questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Incontinence (PDF p. 49)

questions.stem: Which catheter is used for continuous bladder irrigation?
questions.rationale: The three-way Foley has a third lumen for irrigating fluid.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Catheterization (PDF p. 49)

questions.stem: Which catheter size is usually used for an adult female?
questions.rationale: Female Fr 12–14; male Fr 16–18.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Catheter (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: During female catheterization, the catheter slips into the vagina. What should the nurse do?
options: Pull it out and reinsert it
Leave it and insert a new sterile catheter
Use the same catheter after wiping
questions.rationale: Leave it in the vagina as a landmark and insert a new sterile catheter into the meatus.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Catheter (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: How is the penis held during male catheter insertion?
questions.rationale: Holding the penis perpendicular (90°) straightens the urethra.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Catheter (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: How much urine is drained at a time when relieving a distended bladder?
questions.rationale: Gradual decompression of 750–1000 mL at a time prevents shock.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Catheter (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: Where is a male's indwelling catheter anchored?
questions.rationale: Anchoring on the lower abdomen prevents penoscrotal pressure; females are anchored on the inner thigh.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Catheter (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: After Foley removal, within how many hours should the client void?
questions.rationale: Voiding is expected within 6–8 hours; if not by 8 hours, assess for retention.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Removal of Catheter (PDF p. 50)

questions.stem: During a chest x-ray, what is the client asked to do?
questions.rationale: The client stands in front of the film, inhales deeply, and holds the breath while images are taken.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Chest X-ray (PDF p. 60)

questions.stem: Which SpO2 reading is considered normal?
questions.rationale: Normal pulse oximetry is 95% or more; lower values suggest hypoxemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pulse Oximetry (PDF p. 61)

questions.stem: What should be done before applying a finger pulse oximeter?
questions.rationale: Remove false nails and polish; warming the finger improves blood flow.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pulse Oximetry (PDF p. 61)

questions.stem: How much pleural fluid may be removed in the first 30 minutes of thoracentesis?
questions.rationale: No more than 1000 mL is removed within the first 30 minutes to avoid complications such as re-expansion edema.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thoracentesis (PDF p. 62)

questions.stem: After thoracentesis, how is the client positioned for 1 hour?
questions.rationale: Post-thoracentesis, the client sits or lies on the unaffected side for 1 hour.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thoracentesis (PDF p. 62)

questions.stem: In Allen's test, color should return within how many seconds?
questions.rationale: If color returns within 6 seconds after releasing the ulnar artery, collateral circulation is adequate.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Allen's Test (PDF p. 62)

questions.stem: The total air exhaled after a maximal inspiration is the:
questions.rationale: Vital capacity is the maximum air exhaled after maximal inspiration.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pulmonary Function (PDF p. 63)

questions.stem: Which medication should be held for 4 hours before pulmonary function tests?
questions.rationale: Avoid bronchodilators for at least 4 hours and smoking or heavy meals for 4–6 hours.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pulmonary Function (PDF p. 63)

questions.stem: During pulmonary angiography dye injection, what may the client feel?
questions.rationale: Clients may feel burning and flushing, an urge to cough, nausea, or a salty metallic taste.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pulmonary Angiography (PDF p. 64)

questions.stem: Why does the nurse mark peripheral pulses before angiography?
questions.rationale: Marking pulses allows comparison of circulation after the procedure; bed rest is kept 4–6 hours.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pulmonary Angiography (PDF p. 64)

questions.stem: Which older adult finding after bronchoscopy needs attention?
questions.rationale: Older clients are assessed for confusion and lethargy after sedation; NPO until gag returns.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bronchoscopy (PDF p. 61)

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a client wearing a Holter monitor?
options: Keep an activity and symptom log
questions.rationale: The client records activities and presses the button with symptoms, avoids electrical devices and showers, and wears loose clothing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Holter Monitor (PDF p. 68)

questions.stem: How long does a Holter monitor usually record?
questions.rationale: The Holter monitor records cardiac activity continuously for 24 hours during normal activities.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Holter Monitor (PDF p. 67)

questions.stem: Before an exercise stress test, the client should:
questions.rationale: NPO 4 hours, avoid tobacco and caffeine, and wear exercise clothes and rubber-soled shoes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Stress Testing (PDF p. 68)

questions.stem: Which condition contraindicates a stress test?
questions.rationale: Contraindications include unstable angina, severe aortic stenosis, acute myocarditis, severe hypertension, and heart failure.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Stress Testing (PDF p. 68)

questions.stem: After cardiac catheterization, how is the head of the bed kept?
questions.rationale: Bed rest 2–6 hours with HOB no greater than 30°; check the site and distal pulses.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Catheterization (PDF p. 69)

questions.stem: After cardiac catheterization, which assessment of the affected leg is frequent?
questions.rationale: The extremity's temperature, color, and capillary refill and peripheral pulses are checked often.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Catheterization (PDF p. 69)

questions.stem: What is the normal serum creatinine range?
questions.rationale: Normal creatinine is 0.6–1.2 mg/dL; BUN is 7–18 mg/dL.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Serum Tests (PDF p. 74)

questions.stem: Which preparation is ordered before a KUB x-ray?
questions.rationale: A laxative in the evening and an enema in the morning may be ordered; little or no pain is expected.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, KUB (PDF p. 74)

questions.stem: In what position is cystoscopy done?
questions.rationale: Cystoscopy is performed in the lithotomy position after voiding.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cystoscopy (PDF p. 74)

questions.stem: After cystoscopy, which finding is expected?
questions.rationale: Blood-tinged urine, dysuria, and frequency are expected early; fever, chills, or persistent pain are reported.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cystoscopy (PDF p. 74)

questions.stem: Which comfort measure helps after cystoscopy?
questions.rationale: Warm sitz baths relieve discomfort; fluids are increased.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cystoscopy (PDF p. 74)

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin value is normal for an adult female?
questions.rationale: Normal Hgb: female 12–16 g/dL; male 13–18 g/dL.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CBC (PDF p. 76)

questions.stem: What is the normal adult WBC count?
questions.rationale: Normal WBC is 4,500–11,000/mm³.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CBC (PDF p. 76)

questions.stem: Which factor can alter bone marrow biopsy results?
questions.rationale: Recent transfusions, iron therapy, or cytotoxic agents may alter results; it is contraindicated with bleeding disorders.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bone Marrow Biopsy (PDF p. 77)

questions.stem: Which client is at risk with retrograde ureteropyelography?
questions.rationale: Contraindications include dye allergy, dehydration, renal failure, and multiple myeloma (reduced kidney function).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Retrograde Ureteropyelography (PDF p. 75)

questions.stem: 'What the body does to the drug' describes:
questions.rationale: Pharmacokinetics is drug movement: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion. Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pharmacology Terms (PDF p. 105)

questions.stem: Biotransformation of a drug is also called:
questions.rationale: Metabolism (biotransformation) inactivates drugs, mainly in the liver.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ADME (PDF p. 105)

questions.stem: An undesired, abnormal drug response more severe than a side effect is a(n):
questions.rationale: Adverse reactions are undesired, more severe than side effects, abnormal, and reportable.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Therapeutic Index (PDF p. 105)

questions.stem: Which clinical trial phase establishes whether a new drug is better than the standard?
questions.rationale: Phase I safety and dosage; II effectiveness; III comparison with standard drug; IV post-marketing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Clinical Trials (PDF p. 106)

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to give a medicine another nurse prepared. What should she do?
questions.rationale: Do not administer any medication you did not prepare.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nursing Responsibilities (PDF p. 106)

questions.stem: Which drug group is OTOTOXIC?
questions.rationale: Ototoxic drugs include aminoglycosides, aspirin, chloroquine, and loop diuretics.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Drug Toxicities (PDF p. 106)

questions.stem: Which drug causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol?
questions.rationale: Metronidazole, some cephalosporins, and oral hypoglycemics cause disulfiram reactions.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Drug Reactions (PDF p. 107)

questions.stem: Beta-2 receptors are found mainly in the:
questions.rationale: Beta-1 receptors are in the heart; beta-2 in the bronchi, vascular and uterine smooth muscle.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Adrenergic Receptors (PDF p. 107)

questions.stem: Which effect is caused by SYMPATHETIC stimulation?
questions.rationale: Sympathetic effects: mydriasis, bronchodilation, increased HR, decreased peristalsis, bladder relaxation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ANS Responses (PDF p. 107)

questions.stem: Which drug is used first in anaphylaxis?
questions.rationale: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis, bronchospasm, and cardiac arrest.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Adrenergic Drugs (PDF p. 108)

questions.stem: Combining albuterol with which drug class risks hypertensive crisis?
questions.rationale: Albuterol with MAOIs can cause hypertensive crisis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Adrenergic Drugs (PDF p. 108)

questions.stem: Which antidote is used for norepinephrine or dopamine extravasation/overdose?
questions.rationale: Phentolamine is the antidote for norepinephrine and dopamine overdose or extravasation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Adrenergic Drugs (PDF p. 108)

questions.stem: Non-selective beta blockers like propranolol are used cautiously in which client?
questions.rationale: Non-selective beta blockers can cause bronchospasm; caution in COPD, asthma, and diabetes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Beta Blockers (PDF p. 108)

questions.stem: Which is a CARDIOSELECTIVE (beta-1) blocker?
questions.rationale: Selective beta-1 blockers include metoprolol, atenolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, and esmolol.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Beta Blockers (PDF p. 109)

questions.stem: Bethanechol is given to treat:
questions.rationale: Bethanechol, a direct cholinergic agonist, treats urinary retention and abdominal distention.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cholinergic Agonists (PDF p. 109)

questions.stem: What is the antidote for cholinergic overdose?
questions.rationale: Atropine counters cholinergic overdose (salivation, sweating, cramps). Pralidoxime reverses irreversible cholinesterase inhibitors.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cholinergic Agonists (PDF p. 109)

questions.stem: Pralidoxime is the antidote for poisoning with which agents?
questions.rationale: Pralidoxime reverses irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as organophosphate pesticides.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cholinergic Agonists (PDF p. 109)

questions.stem: Which is a sign of cholinergic excess (SLUDGE)?
questions.rationale: SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urinary incontinence, diarrhea, GI cramps, emesis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cholinergic Effects (PDF p. 109)

questions.stem: After spinal anesthesia, how long is the client kept flat to prevent headache?
questions.rationale: Keep the client flat 6–12 hours after spinal anesthesia to prevent spinal headache.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Local Anesthetics (PDF p. 115)

questions.stem: Which peripheral muscle relaxant facilitates endotracheal intubation?
questions.rationale: Peripheral relaxants such as succinylcholine block the myoneural junction for intubation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skeletal Muscle Relaxants (PDF p. 116)

questions.stem: Digoxin is described as having which effects?
questions.rationale: Digoxin strengthens contraction (+ inotropic) and slows the heart rate (− chronotropic).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Glycosides (PDF p. 120)

questions.stem: A client on digoxin sees yellow-green halos. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: Visual changes with yellow-green halos (xanthopsia) suggest digoxin toxicity.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Glycosides (PDF p. 121)

questions.stem: What is the antidote for digoxin toxicity?
questions.rationale: Digoxin immune Fab (Digibind) is the antidote.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Glycosides (PDF p. 121)

questions.stem: A client on digoxin should report which weight change?
questions.rationale: Daily weights; report a 2-lb (about 1 kg) increase, which may indicate fluid retention.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Glycosides (PDF p. 121)

questions.stem: Losartan belongs to which antihypertensive class?
questions.rationale: Losartan, telmisartan, and irbesartan are ARBs; captopril and enalapril are ACE inhibitors.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antihypertensives (PDF p. 121)

questions.stem: Which teaching prevents orthostatic hypotension with antihypertensives?
questions.rationale: Clients are taught to change positions slowly and follow a low-sodium diet.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antihypertensives (PDF p. 122)

questions.stem: Which is a contraindication to streptokinase?
questions.rationale: Thrombolytics are contraindicated with active bleeding, cerebral hemorrhage, recent surgery, and severe hypertension.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thrombolytics (PDF p. 122)

questions.stem: Which is the antidote for thrombolytic-induced bleeding?
questions.rationale: Aminocaproic acid, a fibrinolysis inhibitor, is the antidote for thrombolytics.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thrombolytics (PDF p. 122)

questions.stem: A client on atorvastatin should report which symptom?
questions.rationale: Statins can cause muscle tenderness or weakness and liver dysfunction; LFTs are monitored.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antilipemics (PDF p. 123)

questions.stem: How is a nitroglycerin patch used to prevent tolerance?
questions.rationale: Remove after 12–14 hours to allow a 10–12 hour patch-free interval; apply to hairless areas and rotate sites.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antianginals (PDF p. 123)

questions.stem: Chest pain persists after 3 sublingual nitroglycerin tablets over 15 minutes. What next?
questions.rationale: Give one tablet every 5 minutes up to three; if no relief after 15 minutes, notify the physician immediately.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antianginals (PDF p. 124)

questions.stem: How often should sublingual nitroglycerin be replaced?
questions.rationale: Replace approximately every six months and protect from heat and light.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antianginals (PDF p. 124)

questions.stem: Which teaching is given for beta blockers?
questions.rationale: Beta blockers are not discontinued abruptly; take the pulse first and take at the same time daily.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Beta Blockers (PDF p. 124)

questions.stem: A client on a calcium channel blocker becomes constipated. What should the nurse advise?
questions.rationale: Increase fluids to counteract constipation; limit caffeine and avoid alcohol.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Calcium-Channel Blockers (PDF p. 125)

questions.stem: Which lab test monitors heparin therapy?
questions.rationale: Heparin is monitored by aPTT (therapeutic 1.5–2.5 times control); warfarin by PT/INR.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anticoagulants (PDF p. 126)

questions.stem: What is the usual therapeutic INR range for warfarin?
questions.rationale: Warfarin is monitored by PT/INR, with a usual therapeutic INR of 2.0–3.0.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anticoagulants (PDF p. 126)

questions.stem: What is the antidote for warfarin (Coumadin)?
questions.rationale: Vitamin K reverses warfarin; protamine sulfate reverses heparin.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anticoagulants (PDF p. 126)

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a client on anticoagulants?
questions.rationale: Use a soft toothbrush, avoid aspirin and IM injections, and report bleeding such as black stools.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anticoagulants (PDF p. 126)

questions.stem: Which drug level is monitored for a client on theophylline?
questions.rationale: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range, so serum levels are monitored.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bronchodilators (PDF p. 128)

questions.stem: After an oral mucolytic, what should the client avoid right away?
questions.rationale: Take no fluids directly after oral administration; otherwise increase overall fluid intake.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mucolytics (PDF p. 129)

questions.stem: How long before allergy skin testing should antihistamines be stopped?
questions.rationale: Discontinue antihistamines four days before allergy skin testing to avoid false negatives.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antihistamines (PDF p. 130)

questions.stem: When a client uses both a bronchodilator and a steroid inhaler, which is used first?
questions.rationale: Give the bronchodilator first to open airways, then the steroid; rinse the mouth after the steroid.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anti-inflammatory Drugs (PDF p. 131)

questions.stem: Why should the client rinse the mouth after a steroid inhaler?
questions.rationale: Rinsing after a steroid inhaler reduces oral candidiasis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anti-inflammatory Drugs (PDF p. 131)

questions.stem: A client on a loop diuretic should report which change?
questions.rationale: Loop diuretics can be ototoxic; report hearing changes and change positions slowly.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Diuretics (PDF p. 134)

questions.stem: Which teaching applies to sulfonamides for UTI?
questions.rationale: Increase fluids (prevent crystalluria) and avoid direct sunlight.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sulfonamides (PDF p. 135)

questions.stem: A transplant client on immunosuppressants should report which early?
questions.rationale: Report early signs of infection such as fever and sore throat; hirsutism is reversible.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immunosuppressants (PDF p. 135)

questions.stem: Why should nitrofurantoin tablets not be crushed?
questions.rationale: Nitrofurantoin stains teeth; dilute the suspension and rinse the mouth after.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anti-infectives (PDF p. 136)

questions.stem: Which teaching applies to fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin?
questions.rationale: Fluoroquinolones cause photosensitivity and dizziness; avoid sun and hazardous activities.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anti-infectives (PDF p. 137)

questions.stem: Which sign suggests superinfection during antibiotic therapy?
questions.rationale: Monitor for superinfection signs such as sore throat, fever, and fatigue.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anti-infectives (PDF p. 138)

questions.stem: Which characteristic describes a benign tumor?
questions.rationale: Benign tumors are encapsulated, well differentiated, slow-growing, and do not metastasize.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Characteristics of Tumor (PDF p. 284)

questions.stem: A malignant tumor of bone tissue is called:
questions.rationale: '-oma' usually denotes benign tumors; sarcomas arise from connective tissue such as bone.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Tumor Nomenclature (PDF p. 284)

questions.stem: In TNM staging, the 'N' refers to:
questions.rationale: TNM: Tumor extent, Node involvement, Metastasis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Grading vs Staging (PDF p. 285)

questions.stem: Classifying tumor cells by how much they resemble the tissue of origin is called:
questions.rationale: Grading classifies cells by differentiation; staging determines size, invasion, and metastasis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Grading vs Staging (PDF p. 285)

questions.stem: In carcinogenesis, altered cells invade adjacent tissue and metastasize during:
questions.rationale: Initiation alters DNA, promotion expresses mutant genes, progression invades and metastasizes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Carcinogenesis (PDF p. 285)

questions.stem: Which is a cancer warning sign the nurse should teach?
options: A sore that does not heal
questions.rationale: CAUTION US signs include a sore that does not heal, unusual bleeding, and a nagging cough.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Warning Signs (PDF p. 285)

questions.stem: Which test confirms a cancer diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Biopsy obtains tissue for cell analysis and is definitive; imaging and markers support diagnosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Diagnostic Tests (PDF p. 286)

questions.stem: Freezing tumor tissue with liquid nitrogen is called:
questions.rationale: Cryosurgery uses liquid nitrogen to freeze and destroy tissue.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgery (PDF p. 286)

questions.stem: A client receiving external beam radiation asks about skin care. The nurse advises:
options: Do not wash off the skin markings
questions.rationale: Keep markings, avoid ointments, lotions, and powders, and protect skin from heat.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, External Radiation (PDF p. 286)

questions.stem: A visitor asks whether a client on external beam radiation is radioactive. The nurse answers:
options: No, the client emits no radiation
questions.rationale: In teletherapy the source is outside the body; the client is not radioactive.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, External Radiation (PDF p. 286)

questions.stem: Which nurse should not be assigned to a client with a cervical radium implant?
questions.rationale: Never assign pregnant staff, and do not allow child visitors, for brachytherapy clients.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Brachytherapy (PDF p. 287)

questions.stem: Which radiation safety principle protects the nurse caring for a client with an implant?
questions.rationale: Limit time, keep distance (about 6 feet), and use shielding with a dosimeter badge.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Brachytherapy (PDF p. 287)

questions.stem: During intracavitary brachytherapy for cervical cancer, which diet is ordered?
questions.rationale: Low-residue diet slows bowel movement to prevent dislodging the implant; bed rest and catheter are used.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Brachytherapy (PDF p. 287)

questions.stem: A client received oral iodine-131 for thyroid cancer. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: With unsealed sources, body fluids are radioactive: flush 3 times and do not share the toilet.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Unsealed Brachytherapy (PDF p. 287)

questions.stem: Vincristine acts on the cell cycle by:
questions.rationale: Mitotic inhibitors (vincristine, vinblastine, paclitaxel) arrest metaphase.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mitotic Inhibitors (PDF p. 288)

questions.stem: Which chemotherapy drug is an antimetabolite?
questions.rationale: Antimetabolites (methotrexate, 6-MP, cytarabine) block enzymes needed for DNA synthesis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anti-metabolites (PDF p. 287)

questions.stem: Which antineoplastic class crosses the blood-brain barrier, useful for brain tumors?
questions.rationale: Nitrosoureas (carmustine, lomustine) cross the blood-brain barrier.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nitrosoureas (PDF p. 288)

questions.stem: Trastuzumab and rituximab belong to which class?
questions.rationale: Monoclonal antibodies target cancer cells while sparing normal cells.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Monoclonal Antibodies (PDF p. 289)

questions.stem: Which practice is correct when preparing chemotherapy drugs?
options: Wear gloves, gown, and face shield
Prepare in a closed small room
questions.rationale: Use full PPE, a well-ventilated area, hazard labels, and leak- and puncture-proof disposal.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Preparing Chemo Drugs (PDF p. 289)

questions.stem: A chemotherapy drug spills on the counter. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Spills are cleaned with a designated spill kit.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Handling Waste (PDF p. 289)

questions.stem: How should antiemetics be scheduled for a client on highly emetogenic chemotherapy?
questions.rationale: Give antiemetics round-the-clock; nausea may last 24–48 hours and recur up to a week later.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nausea & Vomiting (PDF p. 289)

questions.stem: When does chemotherapy-induced alopecia usually begin?
questions.rationale: Hair loss begins 2–3 weeks after starting; regrowth may begin around 8 weeks after therapy.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Alopecia (PDF p. 289)

questions.stem: Which mouth care is appropriate for chemotherapy-induced stomatitis?
questions.rationale: Use saline rinses, a soft brush, and a bland diet; avoid alcohol mouthwash, spicy, and citrus foods.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stomatitis (PDF p. 290)

questions.stem: Why is viscous lidocaine avoided for stomatitis in children?
questions.rationale: Viscous lidocaine can suppress the gag reflex, increasing aspiration risk in children.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stomatitis (PDF p. 290)

questions.stem: A neutropenic client's relative brings fresh flowers. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Neutropenic precautions exclude fresh flowers and raw foods to reduce infection risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Neutropenia (PDF p. 290)

questions.stem: A client with chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia needs to shave. The nurse provides:
questions.rationale: Bleeding precautions: electric razor, soft toothbrush, no enemas, suppositories, or antiplatelets.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thrombocytopenia (PDF p. 290)

questions.stem: Which order should the nurse question for a client with a platelet count of 20,000/mm³?
questions.rationale: Avoid suppositories and enemas because of bleeding risk; use stool softeners.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thrombocytopenia (PDF p. 290)

questions.stem: Which drug is given for chemotherapy-induced anemia?
questions.rationale: Erythropoietin stimulates RBC production; schedule rest periods with activities.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anemia (PDF p. 290)

questions.stem: Clay-colored stools and rapid weight loss in a 70-year-old smoker suggest cancer of the:
questions.rationale: Pancreatic cancer causes abdominal pain, weight loss, glucose problems, and acholic stools from biliary obstruction.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pancreatic Cancer (PDF p. 291)

questions.stem: The Whipple procedure for pancreatic cancer removes the head of the pancreas plus:
questions.rationale: Pancreaticoduodenectomy removes the pancreatic head, gallbladder, common bile duct, and part of the duodenum.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pancreatic Cancer Surgery (PDF p. 292)

questions.stem: Which is a major risk factor for hepatocellular cancer in the Philippines?
questions.rationale: Risks include hepatitis B, cirrhosis, aflatoxin (moldy peanuts or corn), and alcohol.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hepatocellular Cancer (PDF p. 292)

questions.stem: Aflatoxin, a liver carcinogen, is commonly found in:
questions.rationale: Aflatoxin is produced by Aspergillus molds on improperly stored peanuts and grains.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hepatocellular Cancer (PDF p. 292)

questions.stem: After cholecystectomy, which position promotes comfort and breathing?
questions.rationale: Low-Fowler's position, with splinting, deep breathing, and coughing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Gallbladder Surgery (PDF p. 293)

questions.stem: A client has a T-tube after common bile duct exploration. Which finding should be reported?
questions.rationale: Report sudden increases in drainage, jaundice, clay stools, or dark urine.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, T-tube Care (PDF p. 293)

questions.stem: When the T-tube is clamped before meals, the client develops nausea. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Clamp before meals as ordered; unclamp if nausea or vomiting develops.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, T-tube Care (PDF p. 293)

questions.stem: What is the most common presenting symptom of colorectal cancer?
questions.rationale: Change in bowel habits is most common; blood in stools is second.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Colorectal Cancer (PDF p. 293)

questions.stem: Which diet increases colorectal cancer risk?
questions.rationale: High-fat, high-protein, low-fiber diets are risk factors.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Colorectal Cancer (PDF p. 293)

questions.stem: Which tumor marker monitors colorectal cancer recurrence?
questions.rationale: Carcinoembryonic antigen is used for colorectal cancer.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Colorectal Diagnosis (PDF p. 294)

questions.stem: Why is neomycin given before bowel surgery?
questions.rationale: Oral neomycin, plus bowel cleansing and low-residue diet, reduces infection risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pre-operative Interventions (PDF p. 294)

questions.stem: Removal of the tumor, sigmoid, rectum, and anal sphincter (Miles procedure) results in:
questions.rationale: Abdominoperineal resection removes the rectum and sphincter, requiring a permanent colostomy.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Colorectal Surgery (PDF p. 294)

questions.stem: A new colostomy stoma appears dark and dusky. This indicates:
questions.rationale: A normal stoma is red and moist; dusky, brown, or black suggests necrosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stoma Care (PDF p. 294)

questions.stem: When should a colostomy pouch be emptied?
questions.rationale: Empty at 1/3 to 1/2 full to prevent leakage and pouch separation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stoma Care (PDF p. 294)

questions.stem: The client feels cramping during colostomy irrigation. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Stop momentarily when cramps occur, then continue slowly; the bag hangs 12–18 inches above the stoma.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Colostomy Irrigation (PDF p. 294)

questions.stem: How high should the colostomy irrigation bag be hung above the stoma?
questions.rationale: Hang 12–18 inches above the stoma and insert the lubricated catheter 2–4 inches.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Colostomy Irrigation (PDF p. 294)

questions.stem: What is the earliest and most common sign of bladder cancer?
questions.rationale: Painless hematuria is the earliest and most common sign.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bladder Cancer (PDF p. 295)

questions.stem: Which is the strongest risk factor for bladder cancer?
questions.rationale: Smoking and industrial carcinogen exposure are leading risks; men are affected more.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bladder Cancer (PDF p. 295)

questions.stem: In an ileal conduit, urine drains through a stoma made from:
questions.rationale: An ileal conduit uses a segment of ileum as the stoma for urine.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bladder Cancer Surgery (PDF p. 295)

questions.stem: Which skin cancer is most common and rarely metastasizes?
questions.rationale: Basal cell carcinoma is most common with good prognosis; melanoma is deadliest.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skin Cancer (PDF p. 295)

questions.stem: Which mole feature should prompt evaluation for melanoma?
questions.rationale: ABCDE: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter > 6 mm, elevation or evolution.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skin Cancer Parameters (PDF p. 296)

questions.stem: Which person has the highest risk for skin cancer?
questions.rationale: Fair skin, sunburns, and chronic sun exposure are major risks.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skin Cancer Risk Factors (PDF p. 296)

questions.stem: What is the hallmark sign of iron deficiency anemia?
questions.rationale: Fatigue is the hallmark; also spoon nails, pallor, pica, and angular cheilosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Iron Deficiency Anemia (PDF p. 297)

questions.stem: Spoon-shaped nails seen in iron deficiency anemia are called:
questions.rationale: Koilonychia is spoon-shaped nails from iron deficiency.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Iron Deficiency Anemia (PDF p. 297)

questions.stem: How should a client take ferrous sulfate tablets for best absorption?
questions.rationale: Vitamin C increases iron absorption; dairy and antacids decrease it.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Iron Therapy (PDF p. 298)

questions.stem: A client on oral iron reports black stools. The nurse explains:
questions.rationale: Black stools are a common, expected effect of oral iron.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Iron Therapy (PDF p. 298)

questions.stem: Which technique is used for IM iron dextran injection?
questions.rationale: Z-track prevents leakage and skin staining; do not massage the site.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Parenteral Iron (PDF p. 298)

questions.stem: Which is the pathognomonic sign of pernicious anemia?
questions.rationale: Red beefy tongue (glossitis) with paresthesias and loss of proprioception.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pernicious Anemia (PDF p. 298)

questions.stem: Which test diagnoses vitamin B12 malabsorption in pernicious anemia?
questions.rationale: Schilling test: radioactive B12 is given and a 24-hour urine is collected.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pernicious Anemia (PDF p. 298)

questions.stem: A client with pernicious anemia asks how long B12 injections are needed. The nurse says:
questions.rationale: Without intrinsic factor, B12 injections are given monthly for life.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pernicious Anemia (PDF p. 298)

questions.stem: Which client is at greatest risk for folic acid deficiency anemia?
questions.rationale: Risks include alcoholism, pregnancy, low intake of uncooked vegetables, and malabsorption.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Folic Acid Deficiency (PDF p. 299)

questions.stem: The usual oral dose of folic acid for folate deficiency anemia is:
questions.rationale: Folic acid 1 mg daily; IM for malabsorption.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Folic Acid Deficiency (PDF p. 299)

questions.stem: Which antibiotic is linked to aplastic anemia?
questions.rationale: Chloramphenicol, sulfonamides, benzene, radiation, and chemotherapy can cause aplastic anemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Aplastic Anemia (PDF p. 299)

questions.stem: A CBC showing low RBCs, WBCs, and platelets is called:
questions.rationale: Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia from marrow failure.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Aplastic Anemia (PDF p. 299)

questions.stem: Which nursing measure is appropriate for a client with aplastic anemia?
questions.rationale: Protect from infection and bleeding: reverse isolation, no SQ or IM injections, soft brush, electric razor.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Aplastic Anemia (PDF p. 300)

questions.stem: Which condition triggers sickling of hemoglobin S?
questions.rationale: HbS crystallizes and sickles when oxygen tension is low; dehydration, cold, and infection also trigger it.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sickle Cell Anemia (PDF p. 300)

questions.stem: In sickle cell pain crisis, which nursing action is a priority?
questions.rationale: Treat triggers: hydrate, give oxygen, manage pain, and treat infection; avoid cold.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sickle Cell Management (PDF p. 300)

questions.stem: Aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease is usually caused by:
questions.rationale: Aplastic crisis results from parvovirus infection; sequestration crisis results from organ pooling.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sickle Cell Crisis (PDF p. 300)

questions.stem: A child with thalassemia major receives frequent transfusions. Which therapy prevents iron overload?
questions.rationale: Multiple PRBC transfusions cause iron overload, managed with regular chelation (e.g., deferoxamine).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thalassemia Major (PDF p. 301)

questions.stem: Thalassemia major is also known as:
questions.rationale: Severe beta-thalassemia is called thalassemia major or Cooley's anemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thalassemia (PDF p. 301)

questions.stem: A client with a ruddy complexion, pruritus, and splenomegaly has elevated RBCs, WBCs, and platelets. This is:
questions.rationale: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder with elevated cell counts and hyperviscosity.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Polycythemia Vera (PDF p. 301)

questions.stem: What is the primary treatment for polycythemia vera?
questions.rationale: Phlebotomy (initially 500 mL once or twice weekly) reduces blood viscosity.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Polycythemia Vera (PDF p. 301)

questions.stem: Which instruction is appropriate for a client with polycythemia vera and pruritus?
options: Bathe in tepid water, pat dry
questions.rationale: Use tepid or cool baths, avoid vigorous toweling, and avoid iron and aspirin.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Polycythemia Vera Nursing Care (PDF p. 301)

questions.stem: Hemophilia A results from deficiency of factor:
questions.rationale: Hemophilia A: factor VIII; hemophilia B (Christmas disease): factor IX; both X-linked.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemophilia (PDF p. 302)

questions.stem: Why is hemophilia seen almost exclusively in males?
questions.rationale: Hemophilia is an X-linked trait; females are usually carriers.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemophilia (PDF p. 302)

questions.stem: Where does most bleeding occur in hemophilia?
questions.rationale: About 75% of bleeding is into joints (hemarthrosis); intracranial bleeding is most dangerous.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemophilia (PDF p. 302)

questions.stem: Which medication should a client with hemophilia avoid for a headache?
questions.rationale: Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, and herbal supplements; paracetamol is safer.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemophilia Nursing Care (PDF p. 302)

questions.stem: A child with hemophilia has a nosebleed. Which action is inappropriate?
questions.rationale: Nasal packing is avoided because bleeding often resumes when it is removed.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemophilia Nursing Care (PDF p. 302)

questions.stem: Which layer of the heart is responsible for contraction?
questions.rationale: Myocardium is muscle; endocardium lines chambers and valves; epicardium is outer.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Layers of the Heart (PDF p. 303)

questions.stem: Cardiac output is calculated as:
questions.rationale: CO = HR × SV, normally about 5 L/min.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Output (PDF p. 303)

questions.stem: According to Starling's law, increased ventricular filling results in:
questions.rationale: The more the heart fills during diastole, the more forcefully it contracts.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Starling's Law (PDF p. 304)

questions.stem: Increased afterload from severe hypertension causes stroke volume to:
questions.rationale: Higher afterload means more resistance and lower stroke volume.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Afterload (PDF p. 304)

questions.stem: An S3 heart sound in a 60-year-old client most likely indicates:
questions.rationale: S3 suggests heart failure or regurgitation in adults; it may be normal under age 30.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Heart Sounds (PDF p. 304)

questions.stem: The heart's natural pacemaker, firing 60–100 bpm, is the:
questions.rationale: SA node 60–100; AV node 40–60; Purkinje 20–40 bpm.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, SA Node (PDF p. 304)

questions.stem: The QRS complex on an ECG represents:
questions.rationale: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ECG (PDF p. 305)

questions.stem: What is the normal PR interval?
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ECG (PDF p. 305)

questions.stem: A prolonged QT interval places the client at risk for:
questions.rationale: Prolonged QT increases risk of lethal ventricular dysrhythmia such as torsades.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, QT Interval (PDF p. 305)

questions.stem: A prominent U wave on the ECG suggests:
questions.rationale: U waves usually appear when potassium is low.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, U Wave (PDF p. 305)

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of coronary artery disease?
questions.rationale: Atherosclerosis, abnormal accumulation of fats in arteries, is the most common cause.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Coronary Artery Disease (PDF p. 305)

questions.stem: Which CAD risk factor is non-modifiable?
questions.rationale: Non-modifiable: family history, age, gender; others are modifiable.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CAD Risk Factors (PDF p. 306)

questions.stem: Which procedure places a device to keep a coronary artery open and prevent restenosis?
questions.rationale: Stents prevent closure and restenosis; atherectomy removes plaque; laser vaporizes plaque.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CAD Procedures (PDF p. 306)

questions.stem: Why is a high HDL level protective against heart disease?
options: It carries lipids to the liver
questions.rationale: HDL transports lipoproteins to the liver for degradation and excretion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CAD (PDF p. 306)

questions.stem: Which diet is recommended for a client with CAD?
questions.rationale: Low-calorie, low-sodium, low-cholesterol, low-fat diet with increased fiber.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CAD Diet (PDF p. 306)

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has crackles, orthopnea, and pink frothy sputum. Which side is failing?
questions.rationale: Left-sided HF causes pulmonary congestion: dyspnea, crackles, orthopnea, pink frothy sputum.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Left-Sided HF (PDF p. 307)

questions.stem: Jugular vein distention, ascites, hepatomegaly, and leg edema indicate:
questions.rationale: Right-sided HF backs blood into systemic veins, causing JVD, edema, hepatomegaly, ascites.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Right-Sided HF (PDF p. 308)

questions.stem: The most common cause of right ventricular failure is:
questions.rationale: Left-sided failure backs up into the lungs and then the right heart.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Right-Sided HF (PDF p. 308)

questions.stem: Which assessment best evaluates fluid status in heart failure?
questions.rationale: Daily weight and I&O assess fluid overload and treatment response.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, HF Management (PDF p. 308)

questions.stem: In heart failure, angiotensin II worsens fluid overload by stimulating release of:
questions.rationale: Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, retaining sodium and water.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Renin-Angiotensin System (PDF p. 308)

questions.stem: Which ACC/AHA stage describes refractory end-stage heart failure?
questions.rationale: A: at risk; B: structural disease, no symptoms; C: symptoms; D: refractory end-stage.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, HF Classification (PDF p. 307)

questions.stem: A client with heart failure on furosemide should be monitored for:
questions.rationale: Loop diuretics alter potassium; monitor K+ especially with digoxin.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, HF Pharmacology (PDF p. 309)

questions.stem: Which drug class reduces afterload in heart failure?
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril) decrease afterload.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, HF Pharmacology (PDF p. 309)

questions.stem: Which drug strengthens myocardial contractility in heart failure?
questions.rationale: Digoxin is a positive inotrope.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, HF Pharmacology (PDF p. 309)

questions.stem: What is the usual cause of mitral stenosis?
questions.rationale: Mitral stenosis is usually from rheumatic heart disease causing fibrosis and calcification.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mitral Stenosis (PDF p. 309)

questions.stem: A low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex suggests:
questions.rationale: Mitral stenosis has a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mitral Stenosis (PDF p. 309)

questions.stem: Why may anticoagulants be prescribed for mitral stenosis?
questions.rationale: A dilated left atrium and atrial dysrhythmias raise thrombus risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mitral Stenosis Management (PDF p. 310)

questions.stem: A high-pitched blowing systolic murmur at the apex indicates:
questions.rationale: Mitral regurgitation: high-pitched blowing systolic murmur at the apex.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mitral Regurgitation (PDF p. 310)

questions.stem: A water-hammer (Corrigan's) pulse with widened pulse pressure is characteristic of:
questions.rationale: Aortic regurgitation causes bounding pulses and widened pulse pressure.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Aortic Regurgitation (PDF p. 311)

questions.stem: A client with aortic stenosis faints during exertion. This is due to:
questions.rationale: Aortic stenosis causes syncope, angina, and exertional dyspnea from limited output.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Aortic Stenosis (PDF p. 311)

questions.stem: Small painful nodules on the finger pads of a client with endocarditis are:
questions.rationale: Osler's nodes are painful; Janeway lesions are painless macules on palms and soles.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Infective Endocarditis (PDF p. 311)

questions.stem: Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers in infective endocarditis are called:
questions.rationale: Roth spots are emboli-related retinal hemorrhages.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Infective Endocarditis (PDF p. 311)

questions.stem: A client with a prosthetic heart valve is scheduled for tooth extraction. The nurse anticipates:
questions.rationale: High-risk clients receive antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures to prevent endocarditis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Endocarditis Prevention (PDF p. 312)

questions.stem: A client going home on IV antibiotics for endocarditis should be taught to:
questions.rationale: Record temperature daily for up to 6 weeks, keep aseptic IV technique, and report fever.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Endocarditis Home Care (PDF p. 312)

questions.stem: Which is the most common type of myocarditis?
questions.rationale: Viral myocarditis is most common.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Myocarditis (PDF p. 312)

questions.stem: Clients with myocarditis require close monitoring when given digoxin because they:
questions.rationale: Myocarditis increases sensitivity to digitalis; watch for dysrhythmias, nausea, vomiting.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Myocarditis Nursing Alert (PDF p. 312)

questions.stem: Pericarditis chest pain is typically relieved by:
questions.rationale: Pain worsens with breathing or lying flat and is relieved by sitting and leaning forward.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pericarditis (PDF p. 313)

questions.stem: Which is the most characteristic sign of pericarditis?
questions.rationale: A creaky, scratchy friction rub at the left sternal border is diagnostic.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pericarditis (PDF p. 313)

questions.stem: Before pericardiocentesis, the head of the bed is elevated to:
questions.rationale: HOB at 45–60 degrees brings the heart close to the chest wall for needle insertion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pericardiocentesis (PDF p. 313)

questions.stem: Which finding indicates successful pericardiocentesis?
questions.rationale: Expected: decreased CVP, increased BP, loss of pulsus paradoxus, flatter neck veins.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pericardiocentesis (PDF p. 313)

questions.stem: Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade includes:
options: Chest pain, ST elevation, Q waves
questions.rationale: Beck's triad: jugular vein distention, hypotension, distant heart sounds.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Tamponade (PDF p. 314)

questions.stem: Pulsus paradoxus is a systolic BP drop during inspiration of more than:
questions.rationale: Pulsus paradoxus: >10 mm Hg drop during inspiration, seen in tamponade.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Tamponade (PDF p. 314)

questions.stem: Chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest and nitroglycerin in a predictable pattern, is:
questions.rationale: Stable angina is predictable, exertional, and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Types of Angina (PDF p. 314)

questions.stem: Chest pain at rest with transient ST elevation from coronary vasospasm is:
questions.rationale: Variant (Prinzmetal's) angina is caused by vasospasm; calcium channel blockers are used.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Types of Angina (PDF p. 314)

questions.stem: Which activity may trigger angina and should be avoided?
questions.rationale: Heavy meals, cold, exertion, and stress trigger angina.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Angina Triggers (PDF p. 315)

questions.stem: Nitroglycerin relieves angina mainly by:
questions.rationale: Venous pooling decreases blood returning to the heart, reducing workload.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nitroglycerin (PDF p. 315)

questions.stem: Which calcium channel blocker is used primarily for coronary vasospasm?
questions.rationale: Diltiazem is used for vasospasm; metoprolol is a beta-blocker.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Angina Medications (PDF p. 316)

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes MI pain from angina?
questions.rationale: MI pain lasts longer than 30 minutes and is relieved only by opioids.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MI Assessment (PDF p. 316)

questions.stem: Which cardiac marker rises first after myocardial infarction?
questions.rationale: Myoglobin rises within 1–3 hours, earliest but not cardiac-specific.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiac Enzymes (PDF p. 317)

questions.stem: Which ECG change indicates acute myocardial injury?
questions.rationale: MI ECG: ST elevation, T-wave inversion, abnormal Q waves.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MI ECG (PDF p. 316)

questions.stem: Thrombolytic therapy in acute MI aims to:
questions.rationale: Thrombolytics lyse the thrombus, restoring flow and limiting damage.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MI Pharmacologic Therapy (PDF p. 317)

questions.stem: Which cardiomyopathy causes a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle and risk of sudden death in young athletes?
questions.rationale: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: asymmetric LVH, outflow obstruction, sudden death; about half inherited.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (PDF p. 318)

questions.stem: Dilated cardiomyopathy is commonly associated with:
questions.rationale: Causes include alcohol abuse and chemotherapy.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dilated Cardiomyopathy (PDF p. 318)

questions.stem: Septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic shock are all types of:
questions.rationale: Distributive shock results from systemic vasodilation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Shock (PDF p. 318)

questions.stem: A client with massive bleeding from a stab wound is in which type of shock?
questions.rationale: Hypovolemic shock results from loss of blood or plasma.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypovolemic Shock (PDF p. 319)

questions.stem: Shock after a massive anterior-wall MI is classified as:
questions.rationale: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure from MI, HF, or tamponade.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cardiogenic Shock (PDF p. 319)

questions.stem: A client with a cervical spinal cord injury has hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin. This suggests:
questions.rationale: Loss of sympathetic tone below the lesion causes vasodilation and bradycardia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Neurogenic Shock (PDF p. 319)

questions.stem: A client develops wheezing and hypotension minutes after IV antibiotic starts. After stopping the drug, the nurse gives:
questions.rationale: Remove the antigen and give epinephrine for vasoconstriction and bronchodilation; diphenhydramine follows.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anaphylactic Shock (PDF p. 319)

questions.stem: Septic shock is most commonly caused by:
questions.rationale: Septic shock is the body's reaction to bacterial toxins, generally gram-negative.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Septic Shock (PDF p. 319)

questions.stem: Hypertension caused by pheochromocytoma is classified as:
questions.rationale: Secondary HTN has an identifiable cause: renal disease, pheochromocytoma, Cushing's, coarctation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Secondary Hypertension (PDF p. 320)

questions.stem: Which lifestyle factor increases the risk for essential hypertension?
questions.rationale: Risks: high salt, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, inactivity, low potassium, calcium, magnesium.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Essential Hypertension (PDF p. 320)

questions.stem: ACE inhibitors such as captopril lower blood pressure by:
questions.rationale: ACE inhibitors reduce peripheral resistance and aldosterone without reflex tachycardia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ACE Inhibitors (PDF p. 320)

questions.stem: Which diuretic is potassium-sparing?
questions.rationale: Spironolactone spares potassium; loops and thiazides waste it.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Diuretics (PDF p. 321)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old heavy smoker has instep claudication and rubor with absent pedal pulses. This suggests:
questions.rationale: Thromboangiitis obliterans affects young male smokers with claudication and rubor.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Buerger's Disease (PDF p. 321)

questions.stem: What is the most important teaching for a client with Buerger's disease?
questions.rationale: Smoking cessation halts progression.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Buerger's Disease (PDF p. 321)

questions.stem: Raynaud's phenomenon shows which color sequence in the fingers?
questions.rationale: Vasospasm causes pallor (white), cyanosis (blue), then reactive hyperemia (red).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Raynaud's Phenomenon (PDF p. 321)

questions.stem: Which advice helps a client with Raynaud's phenomenon who works in an air-conditioned office?
questions.rationale: Avoid cold and nicotine; keep warm clothing available.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Raynaud's Nursing Care (PDF p. 322)

questions.stem: Virchow's triad of DVT risk includes vessel injury, altered coagulation, and:
questions.rationale: Virchow's triad: vessel wall injury, venous stasis, hypercoagulability.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Venous Thromboembolism (PDF p. 322)

questions.stem: Which measure prevents DVT in a postoperative client?
questions.rationale: Compression stockings, SC heparin or LMWH, and early ambulation prevent DVT.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, DVT Prevention (PDF p. 322)

questions.stem: Which laboratory value is monitored for a client on warfarin?
questions.rationale: Monitor PT/INR for warfarin and aPTT for heparin.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, DVT Nursing Management (PDF p. 322)

questions.stem: When should an ambulatory client apply graduated compression stockings?
questions.rationale: Remove at night and reapply before legs are lowered to the floor in the morning.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nursing Alert (PDF p. 322)

questions.stem: A spindle-shaped aneurysm involving the entire circumference of an artery is:
questions.rationale: Fusiform is symmetric; saccular is one-sided; dissecting splits layers; false is a pulsating hematoma.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Aneurysm Types (PDF p. 323)

questions.stem: The respiratory center in the medulla mainly responds to blood levels of:
questions.rationale: The medulla responds to CO2; carotid and aortic chemoreceptors respond to hypoxemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Respiratory Anatomy (PDF p. 324)

questions.stem: What is the basic gas-exchange unit of the lungs?
questions.rationale: O2 and CO2 diffuse across the alveolar-capillary membrane.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Respiratory Anatomy (PDF p. 324)

questions.stem: Before using a corticosteroid nasal spray for allergic rhinitis, the client should:
questions.rationale: Blow the nose before applying medication for maximal relief.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Allergic Rhinitis (PDF p. 325)

questions.stem: The common cold is highly contagious because the virus is shed:
questions.rationale: Virus is shed about 2 days before symptoms and during the early symptomatic phase.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Viral Rhinitis (PDF p. 325)

questions.stem: What is the drug of choice for bacterial (streptococcal) pharyngitis?
questions.rationale: Penicillin is the treatment of choice; cephalosporins and macrolides are alternatives.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Acute Pharyngitis (PDF p. 325)

questions.stem: Which comfort measure helps a client with acute pharyngitis?
questions.rationale: Warm saline gargles, cool drinks, popsicles, soft diet, and ice collar soothe the throat.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Acute Pharyngitis (PDF p. 325)

questions.stem: After tonsillectomy, which sign most strongly suggests bleeding?
questions.rationale: Frequent swallowing indicates blood trickling down the throat.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Tonsillectomy Care (PDF p. 326)

questions.stem: Which food is restricted soon after tonsillectomy?
questions.rationale: Milk products may be restricted because they coat the throat and increase clearing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Tonsillectomy Care (PDF p. 326)

questions.stem: Which immediate post-tonsillectomy position allows drainage from the mouth?
questions.rationale: Prone with head turned to the side lets secretions drain.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Tonsillectomy Care (PDF p. 326)

questions.stem: Severe sore throat, trismus, and drooling after tonsillitis suggest:
questions.rationale: Quinsy causes trismus, drooling, odynophagia, and possible airway obstruction.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Peritonsillar Abscess (PDF p. 326)

questions.stem: What is the initial sign of laryngitis?
questions.rationale: Hoarseness is initial; aphonia and cough may follow. Rest the voice.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Laryngitis (PDF p. 327)

questions.stem: Which symptom warrants evaluation for laryngeal cancer?
questions.rationale: Persistent hoarseness over 2 weeks, especially in smokers and drinkers.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cancer of the Larynx (PDF p. 327)

questions.stem: Before a total laryngectomy, the nurse should first:
questions.rationale: Total laryngectomy causes permanent voice loss; set up communication before surgery.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Laryngectomy Care (PDF p. 327)

questions.stem: Chronic bronchitis is diagnosed by a productive cough lasting:
questions.rationale: Productive cough at least 3 months per year for 2 consecutive years.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, COPD (PDF p. 328)

questions.stem: A thin client with barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, and minimal cough is described as a:
questions.rationale: Emphysema: pink puffer, barrel chest, weight loss; bronchitis: blue bloater, productive cough.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Emphysema (PDF p. 328)

questions.stem: Which test identifies a genetic cause of emphysema?
questions.rationale: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic cause.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, COPD Diagnostics (PDF p. 328)

questions.stem: Why is pursed-lip breathing taught to a client with COPD?
questions.rationale: Pursed-lip breathing slows expiration and keeps airways open.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, COPD Interventions (PDF p. 329)

questions.stem: Oxygen for a client with COPD is usually given at:
questions.rationale: Low-flow oxygen avoids suppressing hypoxic drive and worsening CO2 retention.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, COPD Interventions (PDF p. 329)

questions.stem: Which meal plan suits a client with COPD who has weight loss?
questions.rationale: Small frequent meals and supplements improve intake without increasing dyspnea.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, COPD Interventions (PDF p. 329)

questions.stem: Which asthma medication is used for quick relief of acute symptoms?
questions.rationale: Short-acting beta2 agonists are quick-relief; the others are long-term control.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Asthma Pharmacology (PDF p. 329)

questions.stem: What are the three most common symptoms of asthma?
questions.rationale: Cough, dyspnea, and wheezing are most common.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bronchial Asthma (PDF p. 329)

questions.stem: Chronic cough with copious purulent sputum, hemoptysis, and clubbing suggests:
questions.rationale: Bronchiectasis is irreversible bronchial dilation with copious purulent sputum.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bronchiectasis (PDF p. 330)

questions.stem: Which technique should the family of a client with bronchiectasis learn?
questions.rationale: Postural drainage and chest physiotherapy help clear secretions.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bronchiectasis (PDF p. 330)

questions.stem: Tracheal deviation away from the injured side with hypotension indicates:
questions.rationale: Trapped air causes mediastinal shift away from the affected side.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Tension Pneumothorax (PDF p. 331)

questions.stem: What is the immediate management of tension pneumothorax?
questions.rationale: Immediate decompression prevents cardiovascular collapse, followed by chest tube.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Tension Pneumothorax (PDF p. 331)

questions.stem: A client has a sucking stab wound to the chest. The nurse's first action is to:
questions.rationale: Close the open wound immediately with an occlusive (petroleum) dressing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Open Pneumothorax (PDF p. 331)

questions.stem: After thoracentesis for pleural effusion, the nurse should:
options: Record amount and send to lab
Lay client flat on puncture side immediately
questions.rationale: Record the amount of fluid aspirated and send it for laboratory analysis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pleural Effusion (PDF p. 332)

questions.stem: Sharp, knifelike chest pain worse on deep inspiration with a friction rub suggests:
questions.rationale: Inflamed pleural layers rub during respiration, causing localized pleuritic pain.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pleurisy (PDF p. 332)

questions.stem: Blood in the pleural space after chest trauma is called:
questions.rationale: Hemothorax may cause hidden blood loss; treated with chest tube and volume replacement.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemothorax (PDF p. 332)

questions.stem: A client with pleurisy has sharp pain on breathing. Which position helps splint the chest?
questions.rationale: Turning onto the affected side splints the chest wall and reduces pleural stretch.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pleurisy Interventions (PDF p. 333)

questions.stem: Accumulation of pus in the pleural space is called:
questions.rationale: Empyema is purulent pleural fluid, often after pneumonia or lung abscess.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Empyema (PDF p. 333)

questions.stem: Pneumonia developing 4 days after hospital admission is classified as:
questions.rationale: Hospital-acquired pneumonia begins more than 48 hours after admission.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pneumonia (PDF p. 333)

questions.stem: Rusty sputum, sudden high fever, and pleuritic pain suggest:
questions.rationale: Bacterial pneumonia: abrupt fever, purulent or rusty sputum, pleuritic pain.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pneumonia (PDF p. 333)

questions.stem: How much daily fluid helps liquefy secretions in pneumonia, unless contraindicated?
questions.rationale: Hydration of 2–3 L/day liquefies secretions.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pneumonia Interventions (PDF p. 333)

questions.stem: A client on antibiotics for pneumonia feels better on day 3. The nurse teaches:
questions.rationale: Finish the entire 7–10 day course; improvement is expected within 48–72 hours.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pneumonia Teaching (PDF p. 334)

questions.stem: The hallmark of ARDS is hypoxemia that:
options: Does not respond to supplemental oxygen
questions.rationale: Refractory hypoxemia with bilateral infiltrates and reduced compliance characterize ARDS.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ARDS (PDF p. 335)

questions.stem: Which ventilator setting usually improves oxygenation in ARDS?
questions.rationale: PEEP keeps alveoli open and usually improves oxygenation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ARDS Management (PDF p. 335)

questions.stem: A client 3 days after hip surgery suddenly has dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachypnea. The nurse suspects:
questions.rationale: Sudden dyspnea and tachypnea after orthopedic surgery suggest PE.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pulmonary Embolism (PDF p. 336)

questions.stem: The nurse suspects pulmonary embolism. What is the first action?
questions.rationale: Nasal oxygen is given immediately to relieve hypoxemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, PE Management (PDF p. 336)

questions.stem: Which test is considered the best method to diagnose pulmonary embolism?
questions.rationale: Pulmonary angiography is the best method; V/Q scan and spiral CT are also used.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, PE Diagnostics (PDF p. 336)

questions.stem: ABG findings in acute pulmonary embolism typically show:
questions.rationale: Hypoxemia with low PaCO2 from hyperventilation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, PE Diagnostics (PDF p. 336)

questions.stem: Barrett's esophagus is significant because it is a precursor to:
questions.rationale: Chronic reflux changes squamous lining (metaplasia), a precursor to esophageal cancer.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Barrett's Esophagus (PDF p. 341)

questions.stem: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
questions.rationale: About 1 million nephrons per kidney filter, reabsorb, and excrete.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nephron (PDF p. 379)

questions.stem: Most water (about 80%) is reabsorbed in the:
questions.rationale: PCT reabsorbs glucose, sodium, and about 80% of water.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nephron (PDF p. 380)

questions.stem: Normal adult glomerular filtration rate is about:
questions.rationale: GFR is about 125 mL/min.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urine Volume Control (PDF p. 380)

questions.stem: Normal adult bladder capacity is about:
questions.rationale: Adult bladder holds 300–500 mL.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urinary Bladder (PDF p. 380)

questions.stem: Which routine urinalysis finding is abnormal?
questions.rationale: Normal urine has no albumin; pH 4.5–8, SG 1.010–1.020, straw/amber color.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Normal Urine Values (PDF p. 381)

questions.stem: Why are women more prone to cystitis than men?
questions.rationale: A short urethra close to the rectum allows ascending E. coli infection.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cystitis (PDF p. 381)

questions.stem: Which teaching helps prevent recurrent cystitis?
questions.rationale: Void after intercourse, void frequently, hydrate, avoid irritants, wipe front to back.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cystitis Management (PDF p. 381)

questions.stem: Which organism most commonly causes cystitis?
questions.rationale: Ascending E. coli infection is most common.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cystitis (PDF p. 381)

questions.stem: Colicky pain radiating from the flank down to the genitalia suggests:
questions.rationale: Ureterolithiasis causes excruciating, wavelike pain radiating to thigh and genitalia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urolithiasis (PDF p. 382)

questions.stem: What is a key nursing action for a client with renal colic?
questions.rationale: Strain urine and save stones for analysis; force fluids about 3 L/day.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urolithiasis Nursing (PDF p. 383)

questions.stem: Allopurinol is prescribed for which type of kidney stone?
questions.rationale: Allopurinol lowers uric acid; a low-purine diet also helps.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Urolithiasis Management (PDF p. 383)

questions.stem: Which stone forms from urea-splitting bacteria?
questions.rationale: Struvite (alkaline) stones are associated with infection.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stone Types (PDF p. 382)

questions.stem: Nocturia, hesitancy, and weak urine stream in a 65-year-old man suggest:
questions.rationale: BPH constricts the urethra causing obstructive symptoms.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, BPH (PDF p. 383)

questions.stem: Finasteride treats BPH by:
questions.rationale: 5-alpha reductase inhibition reduces glandular hyperplasia; terazosin relaxes smooth muscle.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, BPH Management (PDF p. 384)

questions.stem: After TURP, the drainage becomes bright red. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Increase continuous bladder irrigation flow to clear reddish drainage and prevent clots.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, TURP Care (PDF p. 384)

questions.stem: Why is sterile normal saline used for bladder irrigation after TURP?
questions.rationale: Hypotonic fluid can be absorbed, causing water intoxication.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, TURP Care (PDF p. 384)

questions.stem: Which discharge instruction is appropriate after prostatectomy?
questions.rationale: Avoid straining, heavy lifting, prolonged sitting, and long trips; do Kegel exercises.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, TURP Discharge (PDF p. 384)

questions.stem: Fever, chills, flank pain, and CVA tenderness suggest:
questions.rationale: Kidney infection causes systemic signs and costovertebral tenderness.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pyelonephritis (PDF p. 385)

questions.stem: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically follows a strep throat by:
questions.rationale: AGN appears 7–10 days after GABHS infection.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, AGN (PDF p. 385)

questions.stem: What is the pathognomonic sign of acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.rationale: Periorbital edema with hematuria, hypertension, and oliguria.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, AGN (PDF p. 386)

questions.stem: Which diet is ordered for acute glomerulonephritis?
questions.rationale: Restrict sodium, fluid, and protein; give carbohydrates liberally.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, AGN Management (PDF p. 386)

questions.stem: Massive proteinuria with anasarca indicates:
questions.rationale: Increased glomerular permeability causes massive protein loss and generalized edema.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nephrotic Syndrome (PDF p. 387)

questions.stem: Acute renal failure from severe hemorrhage and hypotension is classified as:
questions.rationale: Pre-renal: hypoperfusion; intra-renal: tissue damage; post-renal: obstruction.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Acute Renal Failure (PDF p. 387)

questions.stem: Acute renal failure caused by an enlarged prostate is:
questions.rationale: Urinary tract obstruction causes post-renal failure.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Acute Renal Failure (PDF p. 387)

questions.stem: Urine output below 400 mL/24 h with rising potassium marks which phase of acute renal failure?
questions.rationale: Oliguric phase: <400 mL/day, hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Phases of ARF (PDF p. 388)

questions.stem: During the diuretic phase of acute renal failure, the nurse watches for:
questions.rationale: Output of 3–5 L/day can cause hypokalemia and volume depletion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Phases of ARF (PDF p. 388)

questions.stem: Kayexalate is given in renal failure to:
questions.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate exchanges sodium for potassium in the gut.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ARF Management (PDF p. 389)

questions.stem: Which diet suits a client in oliguric acute renal failure?
questions.rationale: Moderate protein restriction, high carbohydrates, restricted potassium.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ARF Nursing (PDF p. 389)

questions.stem: What is the leading cause of chronic renal failure?
questions.rationale: Diabetes, then hypertension and glomerulonephritis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Chronic Renal Failure (PDF p. 389)

questions.stem: End-stage renal disease (CKD stage 5) corresponds to a GFR below:
questions.rationale: Stage 5 (ESRD) is GFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m².
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CKD Stages (PDF p. 389)

questions.stem: White crystals on the skin of a client with ESRD are called:
questions.rationale: Uremic frost is urea crystallized on the skin.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CRF Manifestations (PDF p. 390)

questions.stem: Anemia in chronic renal failure is mainly due to:
questions.rationale: Damaged kidneys produce less erythropoietin; it is replaced pharmacologically.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CRF Management (PDF p. 390)

questions.stem: Daily fluid allowance in CRF is usually the previous day's urine output plus:
questions.rationale: Allow 500–600 mL more than the previous 24-hour output to cover insensible losses.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CRF Nutrition (PDF p. 391)

questions.stem: Which protein source is preferred for a client with CRF?
questions.rationale: Allow limited protein of high biologic value: eggs, dairy, meat.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CRF Nutrition (PDF p. 391)

questions.stem: Aluminum hydroxide (Amphojel) is given in chronic renal failure to:
questions.rationale: Phosphate binders lower hyperphosphatemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, CRF Nursing (PDF p. 391)

questions.stem: Peritoneal dialysis outflow becomes cloudy. The nurse suspects:
questions.rationale: Normal outflow is clear; cloudy means infection; yellow suggests bladder puncture.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Peritoneal Dialysis (PDF p. 391)

questions.stem: Before peritoneal catheter insertion, the client should:
questions.rationale: Empty bladder and bowel to prevent puncture.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Peritoneal Dialysis (PDF p. 391)

questions.stem: How does the nurse check patency of an AV fistula?
questions.rationale: A thrill and bruit indicate patency; absence suggests clotting.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemodialysis Access (PDF p. 392)

questions.stem: Why are antihypertensives often held before hemodialysis?
questions.rationale: Dialysis removes fluid; combined with antihypertensives it can cause hypotension.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemodialysis Nursing (PDF p. 392)

questions.stem: Which pruritus measure helps a client on hemodialysis?
questions.rationale: Use bath oils, superfatted soap, lotion, and keep nails short.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hemodialysis Nursing (PDF p. 392)

questions.stem: Which sign suggests acute kidney transplant rejection?
questions.rationale: Rejection: decreased output, fever, tenderness, rising creatinine, BP, and weight.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Transplant Rejection (PDF p. 394)

questions.stem: Hyperacute kidney rejection occurs:
questions.rationale: Hyperacute rejection occurs within hours; the kidney must be removed.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Transplant Rejection (PDF p. 394)

questions.stem: What is the most reliable test to confirm kidney transplant rejection?
questions.rationale: Renal biopsy is most reliable.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Detecting Rejection (PDF p. 394)

questions.stem: The major intracellular electrolyte is:
questions.rationale: ICF: potassium and phosphorus; ECF: sodium and chloride.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fluids and Electrolytes (PDF p. 394)

questions.stem: What is the normal serum sodium range?
questions.rationale: Sodium 135–145; potassium 3.5–5.5 mEq/L.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Normal Electrolytes (PDF p. 395)

questions.stem: Movement of water from low to high solute concentration is:
