questions.rationale: Osmosis moves solvent; diffusion moves solute from high to low.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fluid Movement (PDF p. 395)

questions.stem: Why are infants and older adults at higher risk of fluid imbalance?
questions.rationale: Infants are about 80% water; elderly have less muscle and diminished thirst.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fluid Balance Factors (PDF p. 395)

questions.stem: A dehydrated client's hematocrit is likely to be:
questions.rationale: Too little fluid causes hemoconcentration and high hematocrit.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Lab Tests (PDF p. 395)

questions.stem: A client on furosemide has muscle weakness and a U wave on ECG. The likely imbalance is:
questions.rationale: Diuretics cause K loss: weakness, flat T, prominent U wave.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypokalemia (PDF p. 395)

questions.stem: Tall, peaked T waves in a client with renal failure suggest:
questions.rationale: Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves, widened QRS, and V-fib risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hyperkalemia (PDF p. 396)

questions.stem: Which condition shifts potassium out of cells, causing hyperkalemia?
questions.rationale: In acidosis, H+ moves into cells and K+ moves out.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hyperkalemia (PDF p. 396)

questions.stem: A client with SIADH becomes confused and has a seizure. The likely cause is:
questions.rationale: Dilutional hyponatremia causes headache, confusion, seizures, coma.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hyponatremia (PDF p. 397)

questions.stem: Thirst, dry mucous membranes, and irritability with serum Na 152 mEq/L indicate:
questions.rationale: Hypernatremia: thirst, dehydration signs, neurologic irritability.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypernatremia (PDF p. 397)

questions.stem: Prolonged gastric suctioning can cause hypochloremia and:
questions.rationale: Loss of HCl from suction or vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypochloremia (PDF p. 397)

questions.stem: Which ECG change is associated with hypocalcemia?
questions.rationale: Hypocalcemia prolongs QT; hypercalcemia shortens it.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypocalcemia (PDF p. 398)

questions.stem: A client with bone metastases has nausea, weakness, and somnolence. The nurse suspects:
questions.rationale: Bone cancer releases calcium; hypercalcemia causes anorexia, weakness, somnolence.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypercalcemia (PDF p. 398)

questions.stem: Chronic alcohol use and loop diuretics commonly cause:
questions.rationale: Alcohol and diuretics increase urinary magnesium loss.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypomagnesemia (PDF p. 398)

questions.stem: Overuse of magnesium-containing antacids in renal failure may cause:
questions.rationale: Excess intake with decreased excretion raises magnesium: weakness, hypotension.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypermagnesemia (PDF p. 399)

questions.stem: Phosphate and calcium have which relationship?
questions.rationale: High phosphate means low calcium, and vice versa.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Phosphate (PDF p. 399)

questions.stem: Normal arterial pH is:
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Arterial Blood Gases (PDF p. 399)

questions.stem: Which finding suggests fluid volume deficit?
questions.rationale: FVD: flat neck veins, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, concentrated urine.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fluid Volume Deficit (PDF p. 400)

questions.stem: Which IV fluid is used to expand plasma volume in a hypotensive dehydrated client?
questions.rationale: Isotonic solutions (NS, LR) expand plasma volume.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, FVD Management (PDF p. 400)

questions.stem: In fluid volume deficit, BUN is typically:
questions.rationale: BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine in hypovolemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, FVD Diagnostics (PDF p. 400)

questions.stem: A weight gain of 1 kg overnight equals about how much retained fluid?
questions.rationale: 1 kg (2.2 lb) gain equals about 1 L of fluid.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, FVE Management (PDF p. 401)

questions.stem: Distended neck veins, crackles, and bounding pulse indicate:
questions.rationale: Hypervolemia: edema, JVD, crackles, increased BP and CVP.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fluid Volume Excess (PDF p. 401)

questions.stem: Which diuretic may cause hyperkalemia?
questions.rationale: Potassium-sparing diuretics acting in the distal tubule can raise K.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, FVE Management (PDF p. 401)

questions.stem: A client on a sodium-restricted diet should be taught to:
questions.rationale: Read labels and avoid OTC drugs that may contain sodium.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, FVE Management (PDF p. 401)

questions.stem: ABG: pH 7.28, PaCO2 38, HCO3 16. This is:
questions.rationale: Low pH with low bicarbonate and normal CO2 is metabolic acidosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Metabolic Acidosis (PDF p. 402)

questions.stem: Severe diarrhea leads to which acid-base imbalance?
questions.rationale: Diarrhea causes excess bicarbonate elimination.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Metabolic Acidosis (PDF p. 402)

questions.stem: Deep, rapid breathing in metabolic acidosis is the body's attempt to:
questions.rationale: Hyperventilation compensates by lowering CO2.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Metabolic Acidosis (PDF p. 402)

questions.stem: A client with prolonged vomiting has a high pH and high bicarbonate. The nurse identifies:
questions.rationale: High pH and high HCO3 from gastric acid loss.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Metabolic Alkalosis (PDF p. 402)

questions.stem: Which replacement is given for metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia?
questions.rationale: KCl replaces both potassium and chloride losses.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Metabolic Alkalosis (PDF p. 402)

questions.stem: A client with sedative overdose has RR 6/min. Expected ABG imbalance:
questions.rationale: Hypoventilation retains CO2, causing respiratory acidosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Respiratory Acidosis (PDF p. 403)

questions.stem: An anxious client hyperventilates and reports lightheadedness. The nurse expects:
questions.rationale: Hyperventilation blows off CO2; coach slow breathing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Respiratory Alkalosis (PDF p. 403)

questions.stem: Which nursing action helps an anxious client with respiratory alkalosis?
questions.rationale: Slow breathing or rebreathing allows CO2 to accumulate.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Respiratory Alkalosis (PDF p. 403)

questions.stem: A burn with blisters, mottled red base, weeping, and severe pain is:
questions.rationale: Second-degree burns are blistered, weeping, and painful; full thickness is painless and leathery.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Depth (PDF p. 404)

questions.stem: A burn that is dry, leathery, white, and painless is:
questions.rationale: Third-degree burns destroy nerve endings; grafting is needed.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Depth (PDF p. 404)

questions.stem: Using the rule of nines, an adult with burns on the entire front of the chest and abdomen and one entire arm has:
questions.rationale: Anterior trunk 18% + one arm 9% = 27%.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Rule of 9's (PDF p. 405)

questions.stem: For scattered small burns, the size of the client's palm represents about:
questions.rationale: Palm method: palm ≈ 1% TBSA.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Palm Method (PDF p. 405)

questions.stem: Which burn is classified as major regardless of size?
options: Burn of the face or hands
questions.rationale: Burns to face, eyes, ears, hands, feet, perineum, joints, and inhalation or electrical injury are major.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Extent of Burn (PDF p. 405)

questions.stem: A burn method that adjusts body-part percentages by age is the:
questions.rationale: Lund and Browder is more accurate and age-adjusted.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Estimating TBSA (PDF p. 405)

questions.stem: An electrical burn victim needs cardiac monitoring mainly because of:
questions.rationale: Current through the body causes ventricular fibrillation and internal damage.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Electrical Burns (PDF p. 405)

questions.stem: Singed nasal hair, sooty sputum, and hoarseness after a fire suggest:
questions.rationale: These signs indicate smoke inhalation; monitor airway closely.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Smoke Inhalation (PDF p. 406)

questions.stem: Cherry-red skin and headache after a fire in an enclosed room suggest:
questions.rationale: CO binds hemoglobin about 200 times more than oxygen.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Carbon Monoxide (PDF p. 406)

questions.stem: Oxygen for CO poisoning is continued until carboxyhemoglobin is below:
questions.rationale: Give oxygen until COHb is less than 5%.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Carbon Monoxide (PDF p. 406)

questions.stem: In the first 24–48 hours after a major burn, fluid shifts from:
questions.rationale: Increased capillary permeability causes edema and hypovolemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Emergent Phase (PDF p. 407)

questions.stem: Which lab finding is expected in the emergent phase of burns?
questions.rationale: Cell damage releases K; hemoconcentration raises Hct; metabolic acidosis occurs.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Diagnostics (PDF p. 408)

questions.stem: Stress ulcer in a burn client is called:
questions.rationale: Diminished GI blood flow causes Curling's ulcer; Cushing's follows head injury.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, GI Changes in Burns (PDF p. 407)

questions.stem: What is the leading cause of morbidity and death in thermal burns after resuscitation?
questions.rationale: Immunosuppression increases infection and sepsis risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immunological Changes (PDF p. 407)

questions.stem: What is the correct first aid for a fresh thermal burn?
questions.rationale: Cool with water; never ice, ointments, or salves.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Emergency Procedure (PDF p. 408)

questions.stem: A worker splashes an alkali chemical on the arm. The first action is to:
questions.rationale: Remove clothing and irrigate with copious running water.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Chemical Burns (PDF p. 408)

questions.stem: In the RACE fire protocol, what does 'R' stand for?
questions.rationale: RACE: Rescue, Activate alarm, Confine, Extinguish.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Emergency (PDF p. 408)

questions.stem: Using the Parkland formula, a 60-kg adult with 50% TBSA burns needs how much LR in the first 8 hours?
questions.rationale: 4 × 60 × 50 = 12,000 mL/24 h; half (6,000 mL) in the first 8 hours from time of injury.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Parkland Formula (PDF p. 410)

questions.stem: Burn fluid replacement time is calculated from:
questions.rationale: Formulas are calculated from the time of injury.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fluid Resuscitation (PDF p. 409)

questions.stem: Which is the most sensitive indicator of adequate burn fluid resuscitation?
questions.rationale: Urine output of 30–50 mL/h reflects cardiac output and perfusion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fluid Resuscitation (PDF p. 409)

questions.stem: During the acute (diuretic) burn phase, the nurse expects:
questions.rationale: Fluid returns to vessels; K shifts into cells; hematocrit falls.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Acute Phase (PDF p. 409)

questions.stem: Why are IM injections avoided for burn pain in the emergent phase?
questions.rationale: Hypovolemia and fluid shifts make IM/SC absorption unreliable; give IV opioids.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Pain Management (PDF p. 410)

questions.stem: When should analgesics be given before burn wound care?
questions.rationale: Premedicate about 30 minutes before painful procedures.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Pain Management (PDF p. 410)

questions.stem: Which diet supports burn wound healing?
questions.rationale: Hypermetabolism requires high protein, calories, vitamins, and minerals.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Burn Nutrition (PDF p. 410)

questions.stem: Hydrotherapy for burns is limited to 30 minutes or less to prevent:
questions.rationale: Prolonged immersion increases heat and sodium loss through the wound.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hydrotherapy (PDF p. 411)

questions.stem: How should a circumferential burn dressing be applied?
questions.rationale: Wrap distally to proximally; fingers and toes individually.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Wound Dressing (PDF p. 411)

questions.stem: A circumferential arm burn causes weak distal pulses. Which procedure relieves constriction?
questions.rationale: Escharotomy incises the eschar lengthwise to restore circulation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Escharotomy (PDF p. 411)

questions.stem: A client on silver sulfadiazine has a WBC drop on day 2. The nurse knows:
questions.rationale: Transient leukopenia may occur and resolves in 2–3 days.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Topical Antimicrobials (PDF p. 412)

questions.stem: Which topical burn agent penetrates eschar and may cause metabolic acidosis?
questions.rationale: Mafenide penetrates eschar, is painful, and may cause metabolic acidosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Topical Antimicrobials (PDF p. 412)

questions.stem: Silver nitrate dressings require monitoring of:
questions.rationale: Silver nitrate draws electrolytes out; keep dressings wet and monitor Na and K.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Topical Antimicrobials (PDF p. 412)

questions.stem: Which graft provides permanent burn wound coverage?
questions.rationale: Autograft uses the client's own skin; others are temporary.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Wound Closure (PDF p. 412)

questions.stem: Pig skin used as a temporary burn covering is a:
questions.rationale: Xenograft (heterograft) is porcine; allograft is cadaver skin.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Wound Closure (PDF p. 413)

questions.stem: Why are young children at greater risk from burns than adults?
questions.rationale: Thinner skin burns deeper; higher fluid proportion raises fluid and heat loss.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, The Burned Child (PDF p. 413)

questions.stem: Which bone cells dissolve and resorb bone?
questions.rationale: Osteoclasts resorb; osteoblasts form; osteocytes maintain.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bone Cells (PDF p. 442)

questions.stem: The shaft of a long bone is the:
questions.rationale: Diaphysis is the shaft; epiphyses are the ends.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Parts of the Bone (PDF p. 442)

questions.stem: What is the first stage of fracture healing?
questions.rationale: Hematoma, callus, calcification, then remodeling.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bone Healing (PDF p. 442)

questions.stem: Complete bone remodeling after a fracture can take:
questions.rationale: Calcification within about 6 weeks; full remodeling 6 months to 1 year.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bone Healing (PDF p. 442)

questions.stem: The knee and elbow are examples of which joint type?
questions.rationale: Hinge joints bend in one direction; hip and shoulder are ball-and-socket.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Articular System (PDF p. 443)

questions.stem: Pushing against an immovable wall is which muscle contraction?
questions.rationale: Isometric: length constant, tension increases.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Muscle Contraction (PDF p. 443)

questions.stem: A fluid-filled sac that cushions tendons at friction points is a:
questions.rationale: Bursae reduce friction; ligaments bind bones.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Articular System (PDF p. 443)

questions.stem: Which exercise helps a client in a leg cast maintain thigh muscle strength?
questions.rationale: Isometric quadriceps and gluteal setting prevent atrophy without moving the part.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Exercise and Disuse (PDF p. 444)

questions.stem: Which client is not a candidate for MRI?
questions.rationale: Metal implants, clips, or pacemakers contraindicate MRI.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MRI (PDF p. 444)

questions.stem: Before a bone scan, the client should:
questions.rationale: A full bladder interferes with pelvic imaging; drink fluids to distribute isotope.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bone Scan (PDF p. 444)

questions.stem: After knee arthroscopy, the nurse should:
questions.rationale: Compression dressing, ice, extension and elevation; monitor neurovascular status.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Arthroscopy (PDF p. 445)

questions.stem: Normal synovial fluid obtained by arthrocentesis is:
questions.rationale: Normal synovial fluid is clear, pale, straw colored, and scanty.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Arthrocentesis (PDF p. 445)

questions.stem: How should a wet plaster cast be handled?
questions.rationale: Use palms to avoid dents; leave uncovered on soft surface to dry.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cast Care (PDF p. 448)

questions.stem: How long does a plaster cast take to dry completely?
questions.rationale: Plaster: 24–72 hours; fiberglass dries in 10–15 minutes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Casting Materials (PDF p. 447)

questions.stem: A client with a new cast reports warmth during application. The nurse explains:
questions.rationale: Prepare the client for warmth as the cast sets.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cast Care (PDF p. 448)

questions.stem: A client with a cast complains of itching underneath. The nurse advises:
questions.rationale: Use cool air from a hair dryer; never insert objects.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cast Care (PDF p. 448)

questions.stem: A client in a cast has pain unrelieved by elevation and analgesics. The nurse suspects:
questions.rationale: Unrelieved pain may indicate compartment syndrome; report immediately.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cast Care (PDF p. 448)

questions.stem: For suspected compartment syndrome under a cast, the extremity should be:
questions.rationale: Elevate no higher than heart level; bivalve the cast; fasciotomy may be needed.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Compartment Syndrome (PDF p. 450)

questions.stem: Cutting a cast lengthwise into two halves to relieve tightness is:
questions.rationale: Bivalving relieves tightness; windowing allows wound inspection.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cast Techniques (PDF p. 447)

questions.stem: A warm spot on the cast with foul odor suggests:
questions.rationale: Warmth, drainage, and odor indicate skin breakdown; window the cast.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pressure Ulcers (PDF p. 450)

questions.stem: Contracture of fingers and wrist from obstructed forearm arterial flow is:
questions.rationale: Volkmann's ischemic contracture is a type of compartment syndrome.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immobilized Extremities (PDF p. 450)

questions.stem: Which brace is used for scoliosis?
questions.rationale: Milwaukee brace treats scoliosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Braces (PDF p. 449)

questions.stem: A Dennis Browne splint is used for:
questions.rationale: Dennis Browne shoe corrects talipes equinovarus.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Braces (PDF p. 449)

questions.stem: A cock-up splint is applied for:
questions.rationale: Cock-up splint supports the wrist in radial nerve palsy.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Splints (PDF p. 448)

questions.stem: Which finding in a casted limb is normal?
questions.rationale: Normal: minimal edema, pink, warm, rapid capillary refill, normal sensation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Neurovascular Checks (PDF p. 449)

questions.stem: A client in a long leg cast cannot dorsiflex the foot. Which nerve is likely compressed?
questions.rationale: Pressure on the peroneal nerve causes footdrop.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immobilized Extremities (PDF p. 451)

questions.stem: A client in a body spica cast has abdominal distention and vomiting. The nurse suspects:
questions.rationale: Cast syndrome (superior mesenteric artery compression) causes ileus; NG decompression, IV fluids.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Spica Body Cast (PDF p. 451)

questions.stem: Which action is outside the nurse's role for an external fixator?
questions.rationale: The nurse never adjusts clamps; that is the physician's responsibility.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, External Fixator (PDF p. 451)

questions.stem: Which solution is recommended for skeletal pin site care?
questions.rationale: Chlorhexidine is most effective; water is an alternative.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skeletal Traction (PDF p. 454)

questions.stem: Which finding shows traction is applied correctly?
options: Client slid to foot of bed
questions.rationale: Weights hang freely, ropes unobstructed, client centered, knots away from pulleys.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Traction Principles (PDF p. 452)

questions.stem: Removing weights from skeletal traction is allowed only:
questions.rationale: Skeletal traction is never interrupted except in emergencies.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skeletal Traction Alert (PDF p. 454)

questions.stem: Buck's extension traction is used for:
questions.rationale: Buck's is skin traction to the lower leg before hip or femur surgery.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skin Traction (PDF p. 452)

questions.stem: A client in Buck's traction reports burning under the boot. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Burning may indicate nerve damage or skin breakdown.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skin Traction (PDF p. 452)

questions.stem: Crutchfield tongs provide traction for:
questions.rationale: Crutchfield tongs are skeletal traction for cervical spine.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skeletal Traction (PDF p. 453)

questions.stem: Which exercise reduces venous stasis in a client in traction?
questions.rationale: Active ankle flexion-extension and calf pumping 10 times an hour.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skeletal Traction (PDF p. 454)

questions.stem: After total hip replacement, the leg should be kept in:
questions.rationale: Abduction pillow prevents dislocation; never flex hip over 90 degrees.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Total Hip Replacement (PDF p. 456)

questions.stem: Which statement shows understanding after hip replacement?
options: I'll use a raised toilet seat
questions.rationale: Raised seats limit hip flexion; avoid crossing legs and bending at waist.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Total Hip Replacement (PDF p. 456)

questions.stem: Prophylactic antibiotics before joint replacement are most effective when given:
questions.rationale: Antibiotics within 60 minutes before incision prevent infection.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Orthopedic Surgery (PDF p. 456)

questions.stem: After hip replacement, which drug class prevents DVT?
questions.rationale: Enoxaparin, fondaparinux, stockings, and early ambulation prevent DVT.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Total Hip Replacement (PDF p. 457)

questions.stem: A continuous passive motion device after knee replacement is used to:
questions.rationale: CPM increases circulation and knee range of motion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Total Knee Replacement (PDF p. 457)

questions.stem: The level of amputation is chosen as:
options: Most distal point that will heal
questions.rationale: Preserve length and function; based on circulation and prosthesis fit.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Amputation (PDF p. 457)

questions.stem: A client says he feels his amputated foot cramping. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Phantom limb pain is real; acknowledge it, keep active, use distraction and desensitization.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Amputation Nursing (PDF p. 458)

questions.stem: To prevent hip flexion contracture after above-knee amputation, the nurse should:
questions.rationale: Prone positioning prevents flexion contracture; avoid pillows under stump and abduction.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Amputation Nursing (PDF p. 458)

questions.stem: Why is the residual limb wrapped with an elastic bandage?
questions.rationale: Compression controls edema and shapes the stump for prosthesis fit.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Amputation Nursing (PDF p. 458)

questions.stem: Which item should be at the bedside of a client after amputation?
questions.rationale: A tourniquet in plain sight is needed for massive hemorrhage.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Amputation Complications (PDF p. 459)

questions.stem: During passive ROM, a spastic muscle resists movement. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Stop temporarily, apply slow gentle pressure until relaxation, then continue.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Passive ROM (PDF p. 459)

questions.stem: A client with left leg weakness uses a cane. Which hand holds the cane?
questions.rationale: Hold the cane on the stronger side; move cane with weak leg.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Canes (PDF p. 459)

questions.stem: Crutch users should bear weight on the:
questions.rationale: Axillary pressure can injure the radial nerve (crutch palsy).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Crutches (PDF p. 460)

questions.stem: Properly fitted axillary crutches leave a gap below the axilla of about:
questions.rationale: Shoulder rest 2.5–5 cm (2–3 finger widths) below axilla; elbow flexed about 30 degrees.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Measuring Crutches (PDF p. 460)

questions.stem: Which crutch gait is safest, keeping three points of support?
questions.rationale: Four-point is most elementary and safest; requires weight bearing on both legs.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Crutch Gaits (PDF p. 460)

questions.stem: A client who cannot bear weight on one leg should use which gait?
questions.rationale: Three-point: both crutches and weak leg advance, then the strong leg.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Crutch Gaits (PDF p. 460)

questions.stem: Going up stairs on crutches, the client first moves the:
questions.rationale: Up with the good, down with the bad; affected leg always supported by crutches.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Crutches on Stairs (PDF p. 461)

questions.stem: Which teaching helps a client with acute low back pain?
questions.rationale: Avoid twisting, bending, lifting; limit sitting; firm mattress; short bed rest.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Low Back Pain (PDF p. 461)

questions.stem: Tingling when the nurse taps over the median nerve at the wrist is:
questions.rationale: Tinel's sign suggests carpal tunnel; Phalen's uses forced wrist flexion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Carpal Tunnel (PDF p. 462)

questions.stem: Carpal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the:
questions.rationale: Median nerve entrapment from repetitive wrist movement.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Carpal Tunnel (PDF p. 462)

questions.stem: Progressive contracture of the palmar fascia flexing the ring and little fingers is:
questions.rationale: Dupuytren's: palmar fascia contracture, common in men over 50.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dupuytren's Disease (PDF p. 463)

questions.stem: Which is a risk factor for osteoporosis?
questions.rationale: Risks: postmenopausal women, Asian, sedentary, corticosteroids, carbonated drinks.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteoporosis (PDF p. 463)

questions.stem: Which test diagnoses osteoporosis?
questions.rationale: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry; plain x-ray misses early loss.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteoporosis Diagnosis (PDF p. 464)

questions.stem: Which exercise best helps prevent osteoporosis?
questions.rationale: Weight-bearing exercise like walking promotes bone formation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteoporosis Treatment (PDF p. 464)

questions.stem: Osteomalacia is primarily caused by deficiency of:
questions.rationale: Lack of calcitriol impairs calcium absorption and bone mineralization.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteomalacia (PDF p. 464)

questions.stem: Why is sunlight exposure recommended in osteomalacia?
questions.rationale: UV light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin into vitamin D.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteomalacia (PDF p. 465)

questions.stem: A client reports his hat no longer fits and has bowed legs. This suggests:
questions.rationale: Paget's: rapid bone turnover, skull enlargement, bowing, high alkaline phosphatase.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Paget's Disease (PDF p. 465)

questions.stem: Which lab finding is typical of Paget's disease?
questions.rationale: Elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Paget's Diagnostics (PDF p. 465)

questions.stem: The most common cause of osteomyelitis is:
questions.rationale: S. aureus is most common.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteomyelitis (PDF p. 466)

questions.stem: Why is osteomyelitis difficult to eradicate?
questions.rationale: Avascular infected bone limits immune response and antibiotic penetration.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteomyelitis Facts (PDF p. 466)

questions.stem: IV antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis usually continues for:
questions.rationale: IV antibiotics for 3–6 weeks; chronic cases may need debridement.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteomyelitis Therapy (PDF p. 466)

questions.stem: Bilateral, symmetric joint swelling with prolonged morning stiffness suggests:
questions.rationale: RA is systemic and symmetric with synovial inflammation and pannus.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Rheumatoid Arthritis (PDF p. 467)

questions.stem: Rheumatoid arthritis is best described as:
questions.rationale: RA is a faulty immune response attacking synovium.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Rheumatoid Arthritis (PDF p. 467)

questions.stem: Which is the initial analgesic for osteoarthritis?
questions.rationale: Acetaminophen first, then NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, intra-articular steroids.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteoarthritis (PDF p. 468)

questions.stem: Which teaching best reduces knee pain in an obese client with osteoarthritis?
questions.rationale: Weight loss and moderate exercise reduce joint stress and disability.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Osteoarthritis (PDF p. 468)

questions.stem: Sudden excruciating pain and redness of the big toe suggests:
questions.rationale: Podagra: urate crystal deposition in the great toe.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Gout (PDF p. 468)

questions.stem: Which drug is used for an acute gout attack?
questions.rationale: Colchicine and NSAIDs for acute attacks; allopurinol for chronic gout.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Gout Treatment (PDF p. 468)

questions.stem: Which food should a client with gout limit?
questions.rationale: High-purine foods: organ meats, sardines, anchovies, mackerel; also avoid alcohol.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Gout Nursing (PDF p. 468)

questions.stem: A client with gout should drink about how much fluid daily?
questions.rationale: About 3 L/day prevents uric acid crystallization in the kidneys.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Gout Nursing (PDF p. 468)

questions.stem: A fracture where bone breaks through the skin is:
questions.rationale: Open fractures break the skin; greenstick is incomplete; comminuted has fragments.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fractures (PDF p. 470)

questions.stem: When splinting a suspected fracture, the nurse should immobilize:
questions.rationale: Immobilize joints proximal and distal to prevent fragment movement.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Fracture Emergency (PDF p. 470)

questions.stem: The most common primary malignant bone tumor in adolescents is:
questions.rationale: Osteosarcoma affects rapidly growing bones (distal femur, proximal tibia).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Malignant Bone Tumors (PDF p. 470)

questions.stem: A client with bone metastases from breast cancer becomes lethargic and constipated. The nurse checks:
questions.rationale: Bone breakdown causes hypercalcemia; treat with saline hydration and bisphosphonates.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Metastatic Bone Disease (PDF p. 471)

questions.stem: The intraoperative phase begins when:
options: Client is transferred to OR table
questions.rationale: Intraoperative: OR table transfer until PACU admission.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Perioperative Nursing (PDF p. 485)

questions.stem: Surgery for intestinal obstruction is classified as:
questions.rationale: Emergency surgery requires immediate attention.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Classifications (PDF p. 485)

questions.stem: A gastrostomy tube for a client unable to swallow is which type of surgery?
questions.rationale: Palliative surgery relieves symptoms without curing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Classifications (PDF p. 485)

questions.stem: Who is responsible for obtaining informed surgical consent?
questions.rationale: The surgeon explains and obtains consent; the nurse may witness.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Informed Consent (PDF p. 485)

questions.stem: Which is a responsibility of the circulating nurse?
questions.rationale: Circulator verifies consent, coordinates team, monitors asepsis, and does counts with the scrub nurse.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Team (PDF p. 485)

questions.stem: In which OR zone are masks required at all times?
questions.rationale: Restricted zone requires scrubs, caps, shoe covers, and masks.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Environment (PDF p. 486)

questions.stem: Which part of a sterile surgical gown is considered sterile?
options: Front from chest to table level
questions.rationale: Gowns are sterile in front from chest to sterile field level and sleeves 2 inches above elbow to cuff.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Asepsis (PDF p. 487)

questions.stem: A sterile package's integrity is doubtful. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Items of doubtful sterility are considered unsterile.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Asepsis (PDF p. 487)

questions.stem: Which part of a draped table is considered sterile?
questions.rationale: Only the top surface of a draped table is sterile.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Asepsis (PDF p. 487)

questions.stem: Which process destroys all microorganisms including spores?
questions.rationale: Sterilization is the highest level; boiling and pasteurization do not kill all spores.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sterilization (PDF p. 488)

questions.stem: Which is the most common sterilization method in hospitals?
questions.rationale: Steam autoclave at 121°C is most common.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sterilization Methods (PDF p. 488)

questions.stem: Heat- and moisture-sensitive items are sterilized with:
questions.rationale: Ethylene oxide is used for heat-labile items.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sterilization Methods (PDF p. 488)

questions.stem: Under Spaulding's classification, a vaginal speculum is:
questions.rationale: Semi-critical items contact mucous membranes and need high-level disinfection.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Spaulding's Classification (PDF p. 488)

questions.stem: A urinary catheter is classified as which Spaulding category?
questions.rationale: Critical items enter sterile tissue or body cavities and must be sterile.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Spaulding's Classification (PDF p. 488)

questions.stem: During which stage of general anesthesia may the client have uncontrolled movements requiring restraint?
questions.rationale: Stage 2 (excitement): dilated pupils, rapid pulse, irregular breathing, movement.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stages of Anesthesia (PDF p. 489)

questions.stem: Shallow respirations, weak pulse, and widely dilated pupils during anesthesia indicate:
questions.rationale: Stage 4 medullary depression; stop anesthesia and support breathing and circulation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stages of Anesthesia (PDF p. 489)

questions.stem: Spinal anesthesia is usually injected into the subarachnoid space at:
questions.rationale: Usually between L4 and L5, anesthetizing lower extremities, perineum, lower abdomen.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Spinal Anesthesia (PDF p. 490)

questions.stem: If hair must be removed before surgery, the nurse uses:
questions.rationale: Clippers reduce skin injury and infection risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Skin Preparation (PDF p. 491)

questions.stem: A client refuses to remove her wedding ring before surgery. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: If the client objects, secure the ring with tape per policy.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immediate Pre-op (PDF p. 491)

questions.stem: After preoperative sedation is given, the nurse should:
options: Raise side rails, keep in bed
questions.rationale: Client voids before premedication; then stays in bed with rails up.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immediate Pre-op (PDF p. 491)

questions.stem: Which position is used for hemorrhoidectomy?
questions.rationale: Kraske position elevates the hips for rectal procedures.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Positions (PDF p. 491)

questions.stem: Which surgical position is used for vaginal and perineal procedures?
questions.rationale: Lithotomy for perineal, vaginal, urologic, and rectal procedures.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Positions (PDF p. 491)

questions.stem: Which measure prevents intraoperative hypothermia?
questions.rationale: Warm fluids, remove wet drapes, and adjust room temperature.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypothermia (PDF p. 492)

questions.stem: Which scissors are used to cut delicate tissue?
questions.rationale: Metzenbaum is delicate; Mayo cuts heavy fascia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Scissors (PDF p. 492)

questions.stem: Which forceps grasp delicate structures like the fallopian tube without injury?
questions.rationale: Babcock jaws are rounded for atraumatic grasping.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Grasping Forceps (PDF p. 493)

questions.stem: Which suture gains tensile strength when wet?
questions.rationale: Cotton gains strength when wet; silk loses it.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sutures (PDF p. 493)

questions.stem: Which needle point is used for friable tissues like the liver?
questions.rationale: Blunt points suture friable tissue; cutting points for skin and tendon.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Surgical Needles (PDF p. 493)

questions.stem: Which Aldrete score usually allows discharge from the PACU?
questions.rationale: Score 8–10 (activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness, SpO2).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, PACU Discharge (PDF p. 494)

questions.stem: What is the PACU nurse's first assessment priority?
questions.rationale: Maintain airway and respiratory function first.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, PACU Management (PDF p. 494)

questions.stem: Protrusion of abdominal organs through a wound opening is:
questions.rationale: Evisceration is protrusion of viscera; dehiscence is separation of wound edges.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Wound Complications (PDF p. 494)

questions.stem: Bleeding a few hours after surgery when BP returns to normal and dislodges clots is:
questions.rationale: Primary: during surgery; intermediary: first hours; secondary: later from slipped suture or erosion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Classification of Hemorrhage (PDF p. 495)

questions.stem: Bright red blood spurting with each heartbeat indicates:
questions.rationale: Arterial blood is bright red and spurts; venous is dark and flows.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Classification of Hemorrhage (PDF p. 495)

questions.stem: What is the primary intervention for postoperative hypovolemic shock?
questions.rationale: Replace volume, give oxygen, keep warm, monitor closely.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Postop Shock (PDF p. 495)

questions.stem: When should the nurse intervene for postoperative nausea?
questions.rationale: Treat nausea early to prevent vomiting.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nausea and Vomiting (PDF p. 495)

questions.stem: Decreased breath sounds and crackles at the base on day 1 after abdominal surgery suggest:
questions.rationale: Atelectasis results from shallow breathing; turn, deep breathe, use incentive spirometer.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Respiratory Complications (PDF p. 496)

questions.stem: Coughing is contraindicated after which surgery?
questions.rationale: Coughing raises ICP and IOP; also avoided in plastic surgery.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Respiratory Complications (PDF p. 496)

questions.stem: Before the first postop ambulation, the nurse should first:
questions.rationale: Progress gradually: HOB up, sit, dangle, stand with support.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Ambulation (PDF p. 496)

questions.stem: Which action helps prevent postoperative DVT?
questions.rationale: Hydrate, exercise legs, ambulate early; avoid calf massage and knee gatch.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Preventing DVT (PDF p. 496)

questions.stem: Signs of a surgical wound infection include:
questions.rationale: Infection: redness, swelling, warmth, pus, odor, fever.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Wound Infection (PDF p. 497)

questions.stem: A kidney transplant client on cyclosporine should be monitored for:
questions.rationale: Cyclosporine causes nephrotoxicity, hypertension, tremor, hirsutism, and infection risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immunosuppressants (PDF p. 136)

questions.stem: A client on cyclosporine is distressed by increased body hair. The nurse explains:
questions.rationale: Hirsutism is reversible after treatment ends; never stop abruptly.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Immunosuppressants (PDF p. 136)

questions.stem: A client on acyclovir should be taught to:
questions.rationale: Antivirals can be nephrotoxic; increase fluids and complete therapy.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antivirals (PDF p. 139)

questions.stem: Which antiviral is used for influenza?
questions.rationale: Oseltamivir treats influenza; acyclovir treats herpes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antivirals (PDF p. 139)

questions.stem: When infusing IV amphotericin B, the nurse should:
questions.rationale: Use an infusion device, protect from light, and monitor renal function and blood work.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antifungals (PDF p. 140)

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is common during amphotericin B therapy?
questions.rationale: Antifungals cause fever, chills, GI upset, headache, and renal impairment.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antifungals (PDF p. 139)

questions.stem: A client taking griseofulvin for ringworm should be told to:
questions.rationale: Griseofulvin causes photosensitivity.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antifungals (PDF p. 140)

questions.stem: Ceftriaxone belongs to which cephalosporin generation?
questions.rationale: Third generation includes ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ceftazidime; cefepime is fourth.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antibiotics (PDF p. 137)

questions.stem: An aminoglycoside may potentiate which agent during surgery?
questions.rationale: Aminoglycosides potentiate neuromuscular blockade and anesthesia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antibiotics (PDF p. 138)

questions.stem: Which breakfast is appropriate for a 6-year-old with celiac disease?
questions.rationale: Gluten is found in wheat, rye, barley, and oats. Rice and corn are gluten-free and serve as substitute grains.
explanations: Pandesal is made from wheat flour.
Oats are restricted on a gluten-free diet.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 276)

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with heart failure about seasoning food at home. Which should the client avoid?
questions.rationale: Sodium causes fluid retention, so clients with heart failure limit high-sodium condiments such as patis, toyo, and bagoong. Citrus, garlic, and pepper add flavor without sodium.
explanations: Correct: fish sauce is very high in sodium.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 278)

questions.stem: A client with hepatic encephalopathy is choosing lunch from the hospital menu. Which item should the nurse advise the client to avoid?
questions.rationale: The damaged liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, so protein and ammonia-containing foods (meat, poultry, cheese, milk) are limited to prevent worsening encephalopathy.
explanations: Correct: poultry is a high-protein food that raises ammonia.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 353)

questions.stem: A client with a new colostomy complains of gas building up in the pouch. Which food should the nurse suggest to help prevent this?
questions.rationale: Yogurt, crackers, and toast help reduce gas. Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, onions, and peas are gas-forming and are avoided until tolerance is known.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 354)

questions.situation: Mr. Santos, 58, underwent a subtotal gastrectomy (Billroth II) for a bleeding peptic ulcer. He is now tolerating a soft diet and is preparing for discharge.
questions.stem: Which instruction helps prevent dumping syndrome?
options: Lie down for a while after each meal
Drink two glasses of water with every meal
Eat three large meals a day
Choose sweet desserts for extra energy
questions.rationale: Lying down after meals and avoiding fluids with meals slow gastric emptying. The diet is small, frequent, dry meals high in protein, moderate in fat, and low in carbohydrates, without concentrated sweets.
explanations: Correct: lying down slows emptying into the jejunum.
Fluids with meals speed gastric emptying.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 227)

questions.situation: Mr. Santos, 58, underwent a subtotal gastrectomy (Billroth II) for a bleeding peptic ulcer. He is now tolerating a soft diet and is preparing for discharge.
questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after lunch, Mr. Santos becomes dizzy, sweaty, and pale and reports palpitations. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Early dumping occurs 5 to 30 minutes after eating as food rushes into the jejunum, causing vasomotor symptoms: dizziness, sweating, pallor, tachycardia, and palpitations.
explanations: A leak causes pain, fever, and signs of peritonitis.
Ileus causes distention and absent bowel sounds.
Correct: vasomotor symptoms soon after eating are typical.
Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 367)

questions.stem: Which finding should the nurse expect in a client with cholecystitis?
options: Pain in the left lower quadrant
questions.rationale: Blocked bile flow causes clay-colored stools, dark urine, and possible steatorrhea. Pain is in the upper right abdomen, may radiate to the right shoulder, and is triggered by fatty meals.
explanations: Correct: lack of bile pigment lightens the stool.
Tarry stools suggest upper GI bleeding.
Gallbladder pain is in the right upper quadrant.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 558)

questions.stem: A client with a ruptured appendix is being monitored for peritonitis. Which finding supports this complication?
questions.rationale: Peritonitis causes a distended, rigid, boardlike abdomen, diminished bowel sounds, and inability to pass flatus or stool, along with fever and tachycardia.
explanations: Fever, not low temperature, is expected.
Correct: abdominal rigidity is a classic sign.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 562)

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a client with chronic pancreatitis to prevent exacerbations?
options: Eat high-fat meals to regain weight
Take three large meals a day
questions.rationale: Exacerbations are prevented by avoiding alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine and by eating small, bland, low-fat, high-protein meals.
explanations: Correct: alcohol is a major trigger.
Fat stimulates pancreatic secretion and should be limited.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 556)

questions.stem: A client with diabetes mellitus has a blood glucose of 644 mg/dL. Which acid-base imbalance is the client at risk of developing?
questions.rationale: Without enough insulin, cells break down fat for fuel. Ketones from fat metabolism are acids, which can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis.
explanations: Hyperventilation may occur as compensation, but it is not the primary imbalance.
Ketones lower pH; they do not raise it.
The primary problem is metabolic, not respiratory.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 216)

questions.situation: Aling Nena, 52, took prednisone bought without a prescription for her joint pains for several months. She is admitted with a moon face, buffalo hump, and thin skin and is diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome.
questions.stem: Which intervention should the nurse include to detect a common complication of her condition?
questions.rationale: Excess glucocorticoids raise blood glucose and can produce signs of diabetes mellitus, so glucose is monitored. Fragile bones and muscle wasting make vigorous exercise unsafe.
explanations: Cortisol, not epinephrine, is the hormone in excess.
Correct: hyperglycemia is a common complication.
Osteoporosis and muscle wasting make vigorous exercise unsafe.
Protein is needed to counter muscle wasting.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 398)

questions.situation: Aling Nena, 52, took prednisone bought without a prescription for her joint pains for several months. She is admitted with a moon face, buffalo hump, and thin skin and is diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome.
questions.stem: Her daughter says that Aling Nena now cries easily, forgets things, and cannot concentrate. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: 'This shows she is depressed about being in the hospital.'
'These are early signs of dementia unrelated to her illness.'
'This happens when her blood sugar drops too low.'
'Excess cortisol can cause mood and memory changes.'
questions.rationale: Exaggerated glucocorticoid effects in Cushing's syndrome cause mood disturbances, memory loss, and poor concentration.
explanations: This ignores a known effect of her disorder.
These changes are linked to her cortisol excess.
Cushing's causes high, not low, blood glucose.
Correct: mood and cognitive changes are features of Cushing's syndrome.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 406)

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for bilateral adrenalectomy. What should the nurse tell the client about care after surgery?
options: 'You will need adrenal hormone replacement for life.'
'Your hormones will return to normal in a few weeks.'
'You will need a diet very low in sodium for life.'
questions.rationale: Removing both adrenal glands eliminates cortisol and aldosterone production, so replacement is permanent. Afterward the client is watched for acute adrenal insufficiency.
explanations: Correct: without adrenal glands, replacement is lifelong.
The tumor is usually benign; chemotherapy is not routine.
No adrenal tissue remains to recover.
Loss of aldosterone causes sodium loss, so severe restriction is not the plan.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 408)

questions.stem: To prevent Addisonian crisis, which medication does the nurse expect to give in the immediate preoperative period before an adrenalectomy?
questions.rationale: A parenteral glucocorticoid such as methylprednisolone is given just before adrenalectomy to protect against acute adrenal insufficiency.
explanations: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid used for later maintenance.
Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, not a replacement.
Correct: an IV glucocorticoid prevents adrenal crisis.
Potassium does not prevent adrenal insufficiency.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 409)

questions.stem: Which position helps prevent increased intracranial pressure in a client with a head injury?
options: Left Sims' position with knees flexed
Head of bed at 30 degrees, head midline
Flat with the head on a small pillow
questions.rationale: The head of the bed is raised at least 30 degrees with the head midline and neutral, avoiding extreme neck and hip flexion, to promote venous drainage from the brain.
explanations: Side-lying with flexion can impede venous return.
Correct: elevation with a midline head promotes venous drainage.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 372)

questions.stem: An unconscious client with a head injury shows rigid extension of the arms and legs with the wrists pronated. The nurse recognizes this as a sign of:
options: Flaccid paralysis from a spinal injury
Decorticate posturing from a cortical lesion
Decerebrate posturing from a brainstem injury
questions.rationale: Decerebrate posturing, with abnormal involuntary extension, can occur with upper brainstem injury. Decorticate posturing is flexion of the arms. Either one signals deterioration and must be reported at once.
explanations: Flaccidity is a lack of muscle tone, not rigid extension.
Decorticate posturing is flexion of the arms, wrists, and fingers.
Abnormal posturing is never a normal response.
Correct: extension posturing points to upper brainstem injury.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 351)

questions.stem: Which intervention in the care plan of a client with a T3 spinal cord injury helps prevent autonomic dysreflexia?
questions.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia is triggered by bladder or bowel distention or painful skin stimuli. A regular bowel program removes a common trigger.
explanations: Correct: preventing bowel distention removes a trigger.
Turning every 2 hours is needed to prevent pressure injuries.
Fluid restriction concentrates urine and does not prevent distention.
Room temperature is not the main trigger.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 424)

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis had a chest infection and missed several doses of pyridostigmine. The client now has trouble swallowing and breathing. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Myasthenic crisis follows undermedication, infection, or sudden withdrawal of anticholinesterase drugs. Cholinergic crisis follows overmedication.
explanations: Cholinergic crisis follows too much medication.
GBS is a separate ascending paralysis, often after infection.
Correct: missed doses and infection precipitate myasthenic crisis.
Autonomic dysreflexia occurs with spinal cord injury.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 417)

questions.stem: A client has anterior cord syndrome. Which instruction BEST reduces the client's long-term risk of injury?
options: Test bath water temperature before bathing
Use a vibrating massager on the legs
questions.rationale: Anterior cord syndrome causes loss of motor function and of pain and temperature sensation below the injury, while touch, position, and vibration sense are kept. The client cannot feel burns.
explanations: Orthostatic precautions do not address the main sensory loss.
Correct: loss of temperature sensation puts the client at risk of burns.
Vibration sense is preserved and is not a safety issue.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 440)

questions.stem: After open reduction of a leg fracture and cast application, which finding is the nurse's HIGHEST priority?
options: Pain unrelieved by opioids, with numb toes
A warm, damp cast in the first hour
The client cannot void in the first 4 hours
questions.rationale: Compartment syndrome is the top concern after casting. Numbness, tingling, poor nail-bed blanching, and pain unrelieved by opioids signal compromised circulation.
explanations: Itching is common and not urgent.
Correct: these are signs of compartment syndrome.
A new plaster cast is normally warm while it sets.
Retention needs attention but is less urgent than limb ischemia.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 169)

questions.stem: Which finding in a client in Buck's traction indicates a complication?
options: Warm toes with brisk capillary refill
Weak pedal pulses on the affected leg
questions.rationale: Buck's traction is skin traction held with an elastic bandage or boot. Weak pedal pulses mean the wrap is compressing the vessels. Skin traction has no pins.
explanations: This is a normal circulatory finding.
Buck's is skin traction and has no pins.
Correct: weak pulses show vascular compromise.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 163)

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with diabetes tells the home care nurse, 'I'm so frustrated with all these insulin lessons.' What should the nurse do FIRST?
options: Continue the lesson to finish on schedule
Give the insulin for the client this time
Refer the client back to the physician
Find out what is causing the frustration
questions.rationale: Learning is blocked until the cause of the frustration is addressed. The nurse identifies it before going on with teaching or involving the physician.
explanations: A short-term fix that does not build self-care.
Correct: assess the barrier to learning first.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 1196)

questions.stem: A group of staff nurses resists a new method of assigning nurses to units. What should the nurse manager do FIRST?
options: Implement the change anyway and ignore complaints
Hold face-to-face meetings to discuss the issues
Transfer the resisting nurses to other units
questions.rationale: Face-to-face meetings let staff voice their feelings, identify problems, and develop strategies together, which addresses the resistance directly.
explanations: Ignoring resistance does not solve it.
Punitive and does not solve the problem.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 679)

questions.stem: A nurse manager plans to change the unit's documentation system. What is the FIRST step in the change process?
options: Train the staff on the new system
Identify and define the problem to be corrected
Set a date to start the new system
questions.rationale: The change process begins by identifying and defining the problem. If the problem is wrong, the whole plan targets the wrong thing. Goal setting and planning come next.
explanations: Comes after the problem is defined.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 686)

questions.stem: A home care nurse disapproves of a client's lifestyle and leaves the home of a client with HIV without giving care. Which statement about the nurse's action is accurate?
options: The nurse breached the duty to give nondiscriminatory care
Personal autonomy allows the nurse to leave
The nurse acted correctly to avoid conflict
Any personal belief justifies refusing care
questions.rationale: Nurses must care for all clients without discrimination. Personal autonomy does not override the client's rights, and refusal based on personal disapproval of a lifestyle is not acceptable.
explanations: Correct: the nurse failed the duty to care without discrimination.
Autonomy does not apply when it harms the client's rights.
Abandoning the client is not conflict management.
Personal objections to a lifestyle are not valid grounds.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed. (PDF p. 598)

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis is started on pyridostigmine. Which side effect should the nurse ask the client about?
questions.rationale: Pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Overstimulation of neuromuscular receptors causes muscle cramps and small muscle contractions.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q8 (PDF p. 145)

questions.stem: Before giving hydroxyzine by intramuscular injection, what should the nurse tell the client?
options: 'You may feel some pain at the injection site.'
questions.rationale: Hydroxyzine is an antiemetic and sedative. The IM injection can be painful. It causes dry mouth and drowsiness, and IM drugs take about 20 to 30 minutes to work.
explanations: It causes dry mouth, not salivation.
IM onset is about 20 to 30 minutes.
Correct: the injection can be painful.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q70 (PDF p. 215)

questions.stem: How should the nurse instruct a client to take oral bisacodyl for the fastest effect?
questions.rationale: Bisacodyl works fastest on an empty stomach. Taken at bedtime it acts by morning. Milk and antacids can dissolve the enteric coating early.
explanations: Milk can dissolve the coating and does not speed the effect.
Correct: an empty stomach gives the most rapid effect.
Antacids also damage the enteric coating.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q275 (PDF p. 432)

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a client starting levothyroxine for hypothyroidism?
options: Take it in the morning before breakfast
Take it at bedtime to avoid drowsiness
Skip doses on days the pulse is fast
questions.rationale: Levothyroxine is taken in the morning before breakfast, at the same time daily, to prevent insomnia. Replacement is lifelong, and the client monitors the pulse and reports chest pain.
explanations: A fast pulse is reported, not managed by skipping doses.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q294 (PDF p. 456)

questions.stem: A client with diabetes insipidus is on intranasal desmopressin. Which parameter BEST shows that the drug is effective?
questions.rationale: Desmopressin is an antidiuretic hormone analog. Its effect is judged by fluid balance: intake and output, daily weight, and edema.
explanations: Not the main measure of effect.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q339 (PDF p. 507)

questions.situation: Mrs. Garcia, 55, has type 1 diabetes and is admitted for blood sugar control. She receives 8 units of regular insulin subcutaneously at 7:30 AM.
questions.stem: At what time should the nurse be MOST alert for hypoglycemia?
questions.rationale: Regular insulin starts working in about 30 minutes, peaks in 2 to 4 hours, and lasts 4 to 6 hours. Hypoglycemia is most likely at the peak: 9:30 to 11:30 AM.
explanations: Correct: 2 to 4 hours after the dose.
Near the end of its duration.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q370 (PDF p. 538)

questions.situation: Mrs. Garcia, 55, has type 1 diabetes and is admitted for blood sugar control. She receives 8 units of regular insulin subcutaneously at 7:30 AM.
questions.stem: Mrs. Garcia's blood glucose is 62 mg/dL. Which finding does the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Hypoglycemia (below 70 mg/dL) causes hunger, sweating, weakness, nervousness, cool clammy skin, blurred vision, tachycardia, and palpitations. Polyuria is a sign of hyperglycemia.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q381 (PDF p. 550)

questions.stem: A client is prescribed valproic acid 250 mg once daily for seizures. When is the SAFEST time to give it?
questions.rationale: Valproic acid depresses the CNS, causing sedation, dizziness, ataxia, and confusion. A single daily dose at bedtime reduces the risk of injury; a snack lessens GI upset.
explanations: Daytime sedation increases the risk of falls.
Daytime sedation increases the risk of falls.
Daytime sedation increases the risk of falls.
Correct: bedtime dosing reduces injury risk.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q406 (PDF p. 580)

questions.stem: A client's clonazepam dose for a seizure disorder is being adjusted. Which nursing measure is the PRIORITY?
questions.rationale: During initial therapy and dose adjustments of an anticonvulsant, seizure control can change, so seizure precautions are instituted. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
explanations: Correct: seizure risk changes during adjustment.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q440 (PDF p. 620)

questions.stem: Before giving oral pyridostigmine to a client with myasthenia gravis, what should the nurse check FIRST?
options: The ability to swallow, using sips of water
The time of the last bowel movement
questions.rationale: Myasthenia gravis can weaken the swallowing muscles. The first assessment is whether the client can safely take oral medications, such as by trying sips of water.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q447 (PDF p. 627)

questions.stem: A client has taken metoclopramide for a long time. Which finding should the nurse report to the physician IMMEDIATELY?
questions.rationale: Uncontrolled rhythmic movements of the face or limbs suggest tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. The drug is stopped and the prescriber notified.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q451 (PDF p. 631)

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson's disease recently started on levodopa is about to walk. What is MOST important to assess first?
questions.rationale: Parkinson's disease causes orthostatic hypotension, and levodopa makes it worse. Checking postural vital signs before walking the client prevents falls.
explanations: Helpful, but not the most important here.
Helpful, but not the most important here.
Correct: levodopa adds to orthostatic hypotension.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q592 (PDF p. 800)

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson's disease has just started levodopa. When should the client expect symptoms to begin improving?
questions.rationale: Symptoms usually begin to resolve 2 to 3 weeks after starting levodopa; some clients need up to 6 months. Knowing this supports adherence.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q653 (PDF p. 871)

questions.stem: A client with trigeminal neuralgia is started on carbamazepine. Which statement shows understanding of the teaching?
options: 'I will report a fever or sore throat.'
'I can stop it once the pain ends.'
questions.rationale: Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis, so fever and sore throat (signs of infection) are reported. Unusual bruising and bleeding are also adverse effects to report.
explanations: Correct: signs of infection from agranulocytosis.
It is not stopped without the provider.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q710 (PDF p. 932)

questions.stem: A client taking lovastatin for hyperlipidemia needs periodic monitoring of which laboratory test?
questions.rationale: Lovastatin is converted by the liver and is not used in active liver disease. Liver function tests are checked periodically.
explanations: Correct: statins can affect the liver.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q721 (PDF p. 943)

questions.stem: A client on allopurinol for gout asks what to do during an acute attack. The nurse explains that the provider will likely:
options: Stop all gout drugs for a week
questions.rationale: Allopurinol prevents attacks but does not relieve their pain. Colchicine or an NSAID is added for an acute attack.
explanations: Allopurinol does not relieve acute pain.
Aspirin is not used and can raise uric acid.
Stopping all drugs is not the approach.
Correct: colchicine or an NSAID treats the acute attack.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q774 (PDF p. 1004)

questions.stem: Which instruction belongs in the teaching plan for a client taking iron supplements for iron deficiency anemia?
questions.rationale: Milk and antacids reduce iron absorption. Enough fiber and fluids prevent constipation, and natural iron sources such as meat, fish, and poultry are encouraged.
explanations: Correct: milk and antacids block absorption.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q790 (PDF p. 1020)

questions.stem: A client is starting cholestyramine for high cholesterol. Which instruction is correct?
questions.rationale: Cholestyramine is taken with food and mixed with water, juice, applesauce, or soup, never dry. Constipation is a common side effect, and fluid intake is increased.
explanations: It must never be taken dry.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1086 (PDF p. 1368)

questions.stem: A client taking colestipol long-term may need supplements of which nutrients?
questions.rationale: Bile sequestrants bind bile salts, interfering with absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K and of folic acid. Long-term users may need supplements.
explanations: Vitamin C is water-soluble and is not affected.
Correct: fat-soluble vitamins and folic acid.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1087 (PDF p. 1369)

questions.stem: Misoprostol is added for a client who takes NSAIDs regularly. Which outcome shows it is working?
questions.rationale: Regular NSAID use injures the gastric mucosa, causing epigastric pain. Misoprostol is given to prevent this. Diarrhea is a side effect of misoprostol.
explanations: Diarrhea is a side effect, not the goal.
Correct: it protects the gastric mucosa.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1226 (PDF p. 1519)

questions.stem: A client will be discharged once the phenytoin level is therapeutic. Which result meets this goal?
questions.rationale: The therapeutic phenytoin range is 10 to 20 mcg/mL. Lower levels risk seizures; higher levels risk toxicity.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1240 (PDF p. 1533)

questions.stem: A client receives NPH insulin at 7 AM. During which period is hypoglycemia MOST likely?
options: 11 AM to 7 PM, 4 to 12 hours after
questions.rationale: NPH is an intermediate-acting insulin that peaks 4 to 12 hours after it is given, when hypoglycemia is most likely.
explanations: This is closer to the peak of short-acting insulin.
Correct: the NPH peak is 4 to 12 hours.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1264 (PDF p. 1565)

questions.stem: A client with acute gouty arthritis is prescribed indomethacin. Which statement shows the client needs MORE teaching?
options: 'I'll rest when my joint is painful.'
'I'll call if I notice a rash.'
'I'll take a pill only when the pain is bad.'
questions.rationale: Indomethacin is given on a schedule, not as needed. Rest relieves gout pain, a rash may mean hypersensitivity, and gastric distress or swelling is reported.
explanations: Correct answer: it is taken on schedule, not PRN.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1266 (PDF p. 1567)

questions.stem: A client with Addison's disease takes fludrocortisone. Which therapeutic effect should the nurse focus on?
questions.rationale: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid. It makes the kidneys reabsorb sodium and excrete potassium, restoring electrolyte and fluid balance and preventing hypotension.
explanations: Correct: it promotes sodium retention and potassium excretion.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1311 (PDF p. 1613)

questions.stem: How should a client take aluminum hydroxide tablets?
questions.rationale: Aluminum hydroxide tablets are chewed thoroughly so they do not reach the small intestine undissolved. They are taken 2 hours apart from other drugs. Constipation is a side effect, but a laxative is not taken with every dose.
explanations: Antacids interact with other drugs; separate them by 2 hours.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1320 (PDF p. 1622)

questions.stem: Prednisone is newly prescribed. Which drug on the client's record should the nurse discuss with the prescriber?
questions.rationale: Prednisone irritates the GI tract. Aspirin and NSAIDs add to this irritation and are avoided during corticosteroid therapy. Clients on prednisone are also watched for hyperglycemia and hypokalemia.
explanations: Correct: aspirin plus a steroid increases GI injury.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1334 (PDF p. 1636)

questions.stem: Which statement shows a client understands allopurinol therapy for gout?
options: 'I'll put ice on my lips if they swell.'
'I'll drink at least 8 glasses of fluid daily.'
'I'll stop it if I get a rash, then restart.'
questions.rationale: Clients on allopurinol drink about 3,000 mL of fluid daily. Rash, eye irritation, or lip swelling may mean hypersensitivity and is reported. The drug is taken with or right after meals.
explanations: It is taken with or after meals.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1367 (PDF p. 1670)

questions.stem: A client with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is on lansoprazole. Which pain reliever is the SAFEST choice?
questions.rationale: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome causes gastric hypersecretion. Aspirin and NSAIDs irritate the stomach lining, so acetaminophen is used for pain.
explanations: An NSAID that irritates the stomach.
An NSAID that irritates the stomach.
Correct: does not irritate the gastric lining.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1385 (PDF p. 1688)

questions.stem: A client with a gastric ulcer is on sucralfate 1 g four times daily. When should the client take it?
options: 1 hour before meals and at bedtime
questions.rationale: Sucralfate is taken 1 hour before meals and at bedtime so it can coat the ulcer before food and acid irritate it. It can cause constipation.
explanations: Too late to protect the ulcer.
Correct: before meals and at bedtime.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1403 (PDF p. 1709)

questions.stem: When should a client with peptic ulcer disease take propantheline?
questions.rationale: Propantheline is an anticholinergic that decreases GI secretions and is given 30 minutes before meals.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1409 (PDF p. 1715)

questions.stem: A client takes donepezil hydrochloride. Which condition does the nurse expect the client to have?
questions.rationale: Donepezil raises acetylcholine levels and is used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's-type dementia. It slows disease progression.
explanations: Correct: a cholinergic agent for dementia.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1417 (PDF p. 1723)

questions.stem: A client with multiple sclerosis is taking baclofen. Which finding shows a therapeutic response?
options: Full range of motion in all limbs
questions.rationale: Baclofen is a skeletal muscle relaxant that acts on the spinal cord to reduce the frequency and strength of muscle spasms.
explanations: It relaxes muscles rather than increasing tone.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1428 (PDF p. 1737)

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson's disease takes benztropine daily. Which side effect should the nurse specifically monitor for?
questions.rationale: Benztropine is anticholinergic and can cause urinary retention, so intake and output are monitored. The nurse watches for dysuria, distention, small voidings, and overflow incontinence.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1476 (PDF p. 1785)

questions.stem: A client with diabetes insipidus asks what vasopressin will do. The nurse explains that it:
questions.rationale: Vasopressin, an antidiuretic, increases water reabsorption in the renal tubules and decreases urine output. It also causes vasoconstriction and stimulates peristalsis and smooth muscle.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1481 (PDF p. 1790)

questions.stem: A client well controlled on glyburide now has fasting glucose of 180 to 200 mg/dL. Which drug on the record may be the cause?
questions.rationale: Corticosteroids, thiazides, and lithium can reduce glyburide's effect and cause hyperglycemia. The other drugs may enhance its effect.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1482 (PDF p. 1791)

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client to mix regular and NPH insulin in one syringe. Which instruction is correct?
options: Draw up the NPH insulin first
Roll the NPH bottle between the palms
questions.rationale: The NPH bottle is rotated between the hands to resuspend the insulin; shaking causes bubbles that alter the dose. Regular insulin is drawn up first. Bottles in use may be kept at room temperature.
explanations: Regular is drawn up before NPH.
Shaking causes foaming and dosing errors.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1491 (PDF p. 1800)

questions.stem: Metoclopramide four times daily is prescribed for diabetic gastroparesis. When should the nurse schedule it?
options: With each meal and at bedtime
30 minutes before meals and at bedtime
One hour after meals and at bedtime
questions.rationale: Metoclopramide stimulates upper GI motility. Giving it 30 minutes before meals lets it start working before food arrives.
explanations: Too late to prepare the GI tract.
Correct: before meals and at bedtime.
questions.sourceLabel: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1501 (PDF p. 1810)

questions.stem: A client is to take magnesium citrate after barium GI studies. How should it be taken?
options: With a tepid glass of water
Chilled, with a full glass of water
questions.rationale: Magnesium citrate solution is served chilled with a full glass of water and should not stand for long, which flattens the carbonation and makes it less palatable.
explanations: Correct: chilled, with a full glass of water.
