questions.stem: Noisy breathing from mucus in the throat of a dying client is called:
questions.rationale: The death rattle is noisy breathing from mucus collecting in the throat.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Signs of Impending Death (PDF p. 53)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: How can the nurse help a dying client keep a sense of control?
questions.rationale: Supporting control includes letting clients choose the location and timing of care and activities.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Care of the Dying (PDF p. 53)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Why should the nurse repeat information to the family of a dying client?
questions.rationale: The family may not absorb information because of stress and grieving, so it is repeated.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Supporting the Family (PDF p. 54)

questions.stem: Stiffening of the body about 2 to 4 hours after death is:
questions.rationale: Rigor mortis results from lack of ATP and begins about 2–4 hours after death.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Postmortem Care (PDF p. 54)

questions.stem: How fast does body temperature fall after death (algor mortis)?
questions.rationale: Body temperature falls about 1°C (1.8°F) per hour until room temperature.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Postmortem Care (PDF p. 54)

questions.stem: Why is a pillow placed under the head after death?
questions.rationale: A pillow under the head and shoulders prevents facial discoloration from settling blood (livor mortis).
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Postmortem Care (PDF p. 54)

questions.stem: During postmortem care, what is done with dentures?
options: Inserted to give a natural look
questions.rationale: Dentures are usually inserted to give the face a natural appearance, and the mouth is closed.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Postmortem Care (PDF p. 54)

questions.stem: When is suicide risk HIGHEST in a client starting antidepressants?
questions.rationale: Suicide precautions are maintained especially as depression lifts and energy returns.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antidepressants (PDF p. 112)

questions.stem: When are SSRIs and TCAs usually given?
questions.rationale: SSRIs can cause insomnia, so they are given in the morning; TCAs cause drowsiness, so at bedtime.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antidepressants (PDF p. 112)

questions.stem: How long may antidepressants take to show effect?
questions.rationale: Effects may take 2 to 4 weeks; clients are taught not to stop early.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antidepressants (PDF p. 112)

questions.stem: Which food is AVOIDED by a client on an MAO inhibitor?
questions.rationale: Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, beer, wine, chocolate) can cause hypertensive crisis with MAOIs.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MAOIs (PDF p. 112)

questions.stem: Which drug treats MAOI hypertensive crisis per the handout?
questions.rationale: Phentolamine is given in MAOI hypertensive crisis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MAOIs (PDF p. 112)

questions.stem: Which is an early sign of lithium toxicity?
questions.rationale: Toxicity signs include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle weakness, and confusion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mood Stabilizers (PDF p. 112)

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a client on lithium?
questions.rationale: Adequate fluids and normal sodium prevent lithium retention and toxicity; take with meals.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mood Stabilizers (PDF p. 112)

questions.stem: A client on haloperidol has involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements. What is this?
questions.rationale: Tardive dyskinesia is a late EPS with involuntary oral-facial movements.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antipsychotics (PDF p. 113)

questions.stem: Which teaching applies to a client on chlorpromazine?
questions.rationale: Antipsychotics cause photosensitivity; avoid sunlight, alcohol, and hazardous activities.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antipsychotics (PDF p. 113)

questions.stem: Which is an atypical antipsychotic?
questions.rationale: Atypicals (CROQZ): clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antipsychotics (PDF p. 113)

questions.stem: Which teaching applies to benzodiazepines such as diazepam?
questions.rationale: Benzodiazepines are never stopped abruptly; alcohol potentiates them.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anxiolytics (PDF p. 114)

questions.stem: Which condition contraindicates anxiolytics like benzodiazepines?
questions.rationale: Contraindications include hypersensitivity, acute narrow-angle glaucoma, and liver disease.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anxiolytics (PDF p. 114)

questions.stem: Which drug is used for anaphylactic shock?
questions.rationale: Epinephrine treats anaphylactic shock; dopamine and dobutamine treat hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypotension and Shock (PDF p. 125)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Who formulated the concept of the asylum as a safe refuge?
questions.rationale: Pinel and Tuke formulated asylum; Kraepelin classified disorders; Bleuler coined 'schizophrenia'.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Historical Perspectives (PDF p. 236)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Who coined the term 'schizophrenia'?
questions.rationale: Eugene Bleuler coined schizophrenia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Historical Perspectives (PDF p. 236)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: What is the main tool of the psychiatric nurse?
questions.rationale: Therapeutic use of self, introduced by Peplau, requires self-awareness.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Therapeutic Use of Self (PDF p. 237)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: In Johari's window, qualities known to others but not to oneself are the:
questions.rationale: Quadrant II (blind) is known to others, not self; I open; III hidden; IV unknown.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Johari's Window (PDF p. 237)

questions.stem: 'Is there something you'd like to talk about?' is an example of:
questions.rationale: Broad openings let the client take the initiative in choosing the topic.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 237)

questions.stem: 'Of all your concerns, which is most troublesome?' uses which technique?
questions.rationale: Focusing concentrates on a single point, useful when a client jumps between topics.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 238)

questions.stem: A hallucinating client says he hears voices; the nurse says, 'I hear no one else in the room.' This is:
questions.rationale: Presenting reality indicates what is real when the client misinterprets it.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 239)

questions.stem: Client: 'Should I tell the doctor?' Nurse: 'Do you think you should?' This is:
questions.rationale: Reflecting directs the client's thoughts and feelings back to them.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 239)

questions.stem: 'I will sit with you a while' is an example of:
questions.rationale: Offering self makes the nurse available unconditionally.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 239)

questions.stem: 'I notice you are biting your lips' is an example of:
questions.rationale: Making observations verbalizes what the nurse perceives.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 239)

questions.stem: 'What could you do to let your anger out harmlessly?' is:
questions.rationale: Formulating a plan of action helps the client plan for future situations.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 238)

questions.stem: 'Tell me whether my understanding agrees with yours' is:
questions.rationale: Consensual validation searches for mutual understanding of word meanings.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 238)

questions.stem: 'What seemed to lead up to this?' is:
questions.rationale: Placing events in time sequence clarifies relationships between events.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 239)

questions.stem: Client: 'I am way out in the ocean.' Nurse: 'You seem to feel lonely.' This technique is:
questions.rationale: Translating into feelings verbalizes feelings expressed indirectly.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Communication Techniques (PDF p. 240)

questions.stem: Client: 'I wish I were dead.' Nurse: 'Everybody gets down sometimes.' This response is:
questions.rationale: Equating intense feelings to 'everybody' belittles the client's distress.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Non-therapeutic Communication (PDF p. 240)

questions.stem: Why is challenging a delusion ('If you're dead, why is your heart beating?') nontherapeutic?
questions.rationale: Challenging causes the client to defend the delusion more strongly.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Non-therapeutic Communication (PDF p. 240)

questions.stem: Client: 'They look in my head with a TV camera.' Nurse: 'What channel?' This is:
questions.rationale: Literal responses treat figurative statements as fact; focus on feelings instead.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Non-therapeutic Communication (PDF p. 241)

questions.stem: Client: 'I would like to die.' Nurse: 'Did you have visitors last night?' This is:
questions.rationale: Changing the subject takes the initiative away from the client and ignores suicide risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Non-therapeutic Communication (PDF p. 241)

questions.stem: 'Everything will be all right' is which nontherapeutic technique?
questions.rationale: False reassurance devalues the client's feelings.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Non-therapeutic Communication (PDF p. 241)

questions.stem: 'I'm sure your doctor has your best interest in mind' is an example of:
questions.rationale: Defending implies the client has no right to express opinions or feelings.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Non-therapeutic Communication (PDF p. 241)

questions.stem: A client gives many details but eventually answers the question. This is:
questions.rationale: Circumstantial speech includes excessive detail but reaches the point; tangential never does.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thought Disturbances (PDF p. 242)

questions.stem: A client repeats exactly what the nurse says. This is:
questions.rationale: Echolalia is repetition of another's words; echopraxia is imitation of movements.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thought Disturbances (PDF p. 242)

questions.stem: A client keeps returning to the same topic despite attempts to change it. This is:
questions.rationale: Perseveration is persistent adherence to one idea despite topic changes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thought Disturbances (PDF p. 242)

questions.stem: A client says he is afraid of 'grittiz.' Invented words like this are:
questions.rationale: Neologisms are words invented by the client.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Thought Disturbances (PDF p. 242)

questions.stem: A client feels his body belongs to someone else. This is:
questions.rationale: Depersonalization is detachment or strangeness toward oneself; derealization is toward the environment.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Affect Disturbances (PDF p. 243)

questions.stem: A catatonic client stays in an awkward position the nurse placed him in. This is:
questions.rationale: Waxy flexibility is maintaining positions for long periods even when awkward.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Motor Disturbances (PDF p. 243)

questions.stem: An older client fills memory gaps with made-up stories. This is:
questions.rationale: Confabulation fills memory gaps with fantasy believed by the teller, to maintain self-esteem.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Memory Disturbances (PDF p. 243)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: What is the major task of the PRE-orientation phase?
questions.rationale: Pre-orientation: self-awareness, data gathering, planning the first meeting.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nurse-Patient Relationship (PDF p. 244)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Which phase is the longest and most productive?
questions.rationale: The working phase is longest; limit-setting and exploration occur here.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nurse-Patient Relationship (PDF p. 244)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: A client begins treating the nurse like his strict father. This is:
questions.rationale: Transference is the client unconsciously transferring feelings to the nurse; countertransference is the reverse.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Working Phase (PDF p. 244)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: The major task of the orientation phase is to:
questions.rationale: Orientation establishes rapport, trust, roles, and a mutually acceptable contract.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nurse-Patient Relationship (PDF p. 244)

questions.stem: A client on haloperidol develops torticollis and oculogyric crisis. What is given?
questions.rationale: Acute dystonia is treated with IM benztropine or IM/IV diphenhydramine.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Acute Dystonia (PDF p. 245)

questions.stem: Shuffling gait, mask-like face, and pill-rolling tremor on antipsychotics indicate:
questions.rationale: Pseudoparkinsonism mimics Parkinson's; treated with anticholinergics or amantadine.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Pseudoparkinsonism (PDF p. 245)

questions.stem: A client on antipsychotics cannot sit still and paces anxiously. This is:
questions.rationale: Akathisia is inability to sit still with restlessness; beta-blockers or benzodiazepines may help.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Akathisia (PDF p. 245)

questions.stem: Which statement about tardive dyskinesia is correct?
options: It appears in the first day
It is cured by more drug
questions.rationale: TD is often permanent, appears after months of therapy, and involves oral-facial movements.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Tardive Dyskinesia (PDF p. 246)

questions.stem: A client on antipsychotics has high fever, rigidity, and unstable BP. What is FIRST?
questions.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires immediate discontinuation and treatment of hyperthermia and dehydration.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, NMS (PDF p. 246)

questions.stem: Which lab is monitored weekly on clozapine?
questions.rationale: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis; WBC is checked at baseline and weekly.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Clozapine (PDF p. 247)

questions.stem: A client forgets an antipsychotic dose and remembers 6 hours late. What should he do?
questions.rationale: If more than about 4 hours late or near the next dose, omit the forgotten dose.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antipsychotic Responsibilities (PDF p. 247)

questions.stem: Why are TCA prescriptions given in small amounts to depressed clients?
questions.rationale: TCAs are potentially lethal in overdose, so limited amounts reduce suicide risk.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, TCAs (PDF p. 247)

questions.stem: Which antidepressant class is also effective for OCD?
questions.rationale: SSRIs are effective for OCD and have fewer side effects than TCAs.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, SSRIs (PDF p. 248)

questions.stem: Which drug is dangerous to combine with an MAOI?
questions.rationale: MAOIs are not given with other MAOIs, TCAs, meperidine, or CNS depressants.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MAOIs (PDF p. 248)

questions.stem: Which cheese is allowed on an MAOI diet?
questions.rationale: Avoid aged cheeses; cottage, cream, ricotta, and processed cheese slices are allowed.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, MAOIs (PDF p. 248)

questions.stem: Which antidepressant has a higher risk of seizures?
questions.rationale: Bupropion causes seizures at about 4 times the rate of other antidepressants.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bupropion (PDF p. 249)

questions.stem: Which antidepressant can cause priapism?
questions.rationale: Trazodone can cause priapism.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Other Antidepressants (PDF p. 248)

questions.stem: What is the THERAPEUTIC lithium level?
questions.rationale: Therapeutic lithium is 0.6–1.2 mEq/L; above 3.0 may require dialysis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Lithium (PDF p. 249)

questions.stem: Why should a client on lithium avoid heavy sweating?
questions.rationale: Fluid and sodium loss from sweating increases lithium levels rapidly.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mood Stabilizers (PDF p. 250)

questions.stem: Which mood stabilizer can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
questions.rationale: Lamotrigine: SJS; valproic acid: hepatic failure; carbamazepine: aplastic anemia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mood Stabilizers (PDF p. 250)

questions.stem: Which mood stabilizer can cause hepatic failure?
questions.rationale: Valproic acid can cause fatal hepatic failure.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mood Stabilizers (PDF p. 249)

questions.stem: Why is alcohol dangerous with benzodiazepines?
options: One drink may act like three
questions.rationale: Benzodiazepines strongly potentiate alcohol.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anxiolytics (PDF p. 250)

questions.stem: Why must benzodiazepines not be stopped abruptly?
questions.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal can be fatal; stop only under supervision.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anxiolytics (PDF p. 250)

questions.stem: A child on methylphenidate for ADHD should be monitored for:
questions.rationale: Stimulants cause anorexia, weight loss, irritability, and insomnia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stimulants (PDF p. 250)

questions.stem: A child on stimulant therapy should have which monitored for growth suppression?
questions.rationale: Stimulants can suppress growth, so weight and height are monitored.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stimulants (PDF p. 251)

questions.stem: A client on disulfiram should avoid which product?
questions.rationale: Products such as aftershave, cologne, mouthwash, and some cough syrups contain alcohol and can trigger a reaction.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Disulfiram (PDF p. 251)

questions.stem: Disulfiram is best suited for which client?
questions.rationale: Disulfiram is useful for persons motivated to abstain who are not impulsive.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Disulfiram (PDF p. 251)

questions.stem: Why is atropine given before ECT?
questions.rationale: Atropine decreases secretions; succinylcholine relaxes muscles; methohexital is the anesthetic.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ECT (PDF p. 252)

questions.stem: Which is a common short-term effect after ECT?
questions.rationale: Clients may be confused and have short-term memory impairment; reorient them.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ECT (PDF p. 252)

questions.stem: What preparation is needed before ECT?
questions.rationale: NPO after midnight, void, IV access, and informed consent.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ECT (PDF p. 251)

questions.stem: Per the handout, how many ECT treatments usually produce a therapeutic effect?
questions.rationale: Usually 6–12 treatments (up to 15), spaced about 48 hours apart.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ECT (PDF p. 252)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: A woman who never wanted children becomes an over-involved 'super-mom.' Which defense?
questions.rationale: Reaction formation is acting opposite to one's true feelings.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Defense Mechanisms (PDF p. 253)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: A man angry at his boss yells at his wife. Which defense?
questions.rationale: Displacement vents feelings on a less threatening person.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Defense Mechanisms (PDF p. 253)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: What distinguishes suppression from repression?
questions.rationale: Suppression is conscious exclusion; repression is unconscious forgetting.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Defense Mechanisms (PDF p. 253)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: A teen tempted by friends develops sudden blindness without concern. Which defense?
questions.rationale: Conversion expresses emotional conflict as a sensorimotor symptom, often with indifference.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Defense Mechanisms (PDF p. 253)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Which personality component seeks instant gratification?
questions.rationale: The id seeks instant gratification; the superego is conscience; the ego mediates.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Personality Structure (PDF p. 252)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: An adult remembering childhood events with effort uses which level of awareness?
questions.rationale: Preconscious material can be recalled with effort.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Levels of Awareness (PDF p. 254)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Remotivation therapy is unsuitable for which client?
questions.rationale: Remotivation discusses neutral topics for rehabilitative clients, not actively psychotic ones.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Psychotherapeutic Interventions (PDF p. 254)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: What is the ideal size of a therapy group?
questions.rationale: Minimum 3 members; ideal 8–10.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Group Therapy (PDF p. 254)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Dolls are used to help an abused child express feelings. This is:
questions.rationale: Play therapy lets the child experience intense emotion safely through play.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Play Therapy (PDF p. 254)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Which therapy uses free association and dream analysis?
questions.rationale: Psychoanalysis explores the unconscious using free association and dream analysis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Psychoanalysis (PDF p. 254)

questions.stem: How long does a crisis state usually last?
questions.rationale: A crisis is self-limiting, usually lasting 4–6 weeks.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Crisis (PDF p. 255)

questions.stem: Losing a job suddenly is which type of crisis?
questions.rationale: Situational crises are unexpected external events like job loss or death.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Types of Crisis (PDF p. 255)

questions.stem: A community hit by a typhoon experiences which crisis type?
questions.rationale: Adventitious crises include natural disasters, war, and violent crimes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Types of Crisis (PDF p. 255)

questions.stem: What is the nurse's role during crisis intervention?
questions.rationale: The nurse is active and directive in crisis intervention.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Crisis Intervention (PDF p. 256)

questions.stem: How should the nurse support a rape survivor in the ER?
questions.rationale: Provide emotional support, let her set the pace, and give back control; filing charges is her decision.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nursing Care for Rape Victims (PDF p. 256)

questions.stem: What is the main problem in autism spectrum disorder?
questions.rationale: ASD involves impaired social interaction and communication with stereotyped behaviors.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Autism (PDF p. 257)

questions.stem: A child with autism head-bangs during tantrums. What is the priority?
questions.rationale: Safety is priority: helmet, padded walls.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Autism (PDF p. 257)

questions.stem: What is the priority nursing diagnosis for a child with autism?
questions.rationale: Risk for injury is the priority because of self-injury and lack of fear of danger.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Autism (PDF p. 257)

questions.stem: How should the nurse communicate with a child with autism?
questions.rationale: Use short sentences and provide consistent routines.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Autism (PDF p. 257)

questions.stem: When should the last daily dose of dextroamphetamine be given?
questions.rationale: Give the last dose early afternoon to prevent insomnia.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ADHD Drugs (PDF p. 258)

questions.stem: Which approach helps a child with ADHD complete schoolwork?
questions.rationale: Provide a quiet space, break tasks into small steps, and keep routines.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ADHD Interventions (PDF p. 258)

questions.stem: Which food form suits a hyperactive child who won't sit for meals?
questions.rationale: Finger foods let the child eat while moving.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, ADHD Interventions (PDF p. 259)

questions.stem: A child with mild intellectual disability (IQ 55–69) is described as:
questions.rationale: Mild: educable (reading, writing); moderate: trainable; severe: close supervision; profound: custodial.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Intellectual Disability (PDF p. 259)

questions.stem: Which teaching strategy suits a client with intellectual disability?
questions.rationale: Repetition, role modeling, and restructuring the environment help.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Intellectual Disability (PDF p. 259)

questions.stem: A client focuses only on the immediate task and needs help to solve problems. Which anxiety level?
questions.rationale: Moderate anxiety narrows the perceptual field; the person can solve problems with assistance.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anxiety Levels (PDF p. 260)

questions.stem: A client in panic may bolt and run. What is the nursing priority?
questions.rationale: Panic causes loss of rational thought and injury risk; safety comes first, with calm presence and reduced stimuli.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anxiety Levels (PDF p. 260)

questions.stem: Avoiding places where escape may be difficult is called:
questions.rationale: Agoraphobia is anxiety about places where escape or help may be difficult.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anxiety Disorders (PDF p. 260)

questions.stem: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry for a minimum of:
questions.rationale: GAD: persistent excessive worry for at least 6 months.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, GAD (PDF p. 261)

questions.stem: Symptoms after trauma lasting 2 days to 4 weeks suggest:
questions.rationale: Acute stress disorder occurs within 1 month and lasts 2 days to 4 weeks; PTSD persists longer.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Acute Stress Disorder (PDF p. 261)

questions.stem: A client thinks, 'This is only anxiety; it will pass,' instead of 'I'm dying.' Which technique?
questions.rationale: Positive reframing turns negative messages into positive ones.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cognitive Techniques (PDF p. 262)

questions.stem: A client snaps a rubber band on the wrist to interrupt negative thoughts. This is:
questions.rationale: Thought-stopping uses techniques like snapping a rubber band to break negative thought cycles.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cognitive Techniques (PDF p. 262)

questions.stem: 'I feel angry when you turn your back while I'm talking' is an example of:
questions.rationale: Assertiveness training uses 'I' statements to express feelings and needs.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Assertiveness Training (PDF p. 262)

questions.stem: Which treatment gradually exposes a client to a feared object?
questions.rationale: Systematic desensitization progressively exposes the client in a safe setting until anxiety decreases.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Specific Phobia (PDF p. 263)

questions.stem: Which personality disorder is in Cluster A (odd, eccentric)?
questions.rationale: Cluster A: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal; B: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic; C: avoidant, dependent, OCPD.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Personality Disorders (PDF p. 263)

questions.stem: How should the nurse approach a client with paranoid personality disorder?
questions.rationale: Use a formal, straightforward approach without chit-chat or jokes; involve the client in planning.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Paranoid PD (PDF p. 263)

questions.stem: Which defense mechanism is typical of paranoid personality disorder?
questions.rationale: Projection, blaming others for one's difficulties, is characteristic.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Paranoid PD (PDF p. 263)

questions.stem: A detached, emotionally cold client prefers things to people. Which disorder?
questions.rationale: Schizoid PD shows detachment, restricted affect, and few pleasures.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Schizoid PD (PDF p. 263)

questions.stem: A client with antisocial personality disorder repeatedly breaks unit rules. What is the best nursing approach?
questions.rationale: Set limits and enforce rules consistently, without anger or punitive responses.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antisocial PD (PDF p. 264)

questions.stem: 'You say you want to manage your anger, but you've missed the group meetings.' This nurse response uses:
questions.rationale: Confrontation manages manipulative or deceptive behavior by pointing out inconsistencies.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antisocial PD (PDF p. 264)

questions.stem: Which characteristic is typical of antisocial personality disorder?
questions.rationale: Antisocial PD: violation of others' rights, lying, rationalization, thrill-seeking, irresponsibility.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Antisocial PD (PDF p. 264)

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder has cuts on her forearms. What is the nursing priority?
questions.rationale: Recurrent self-mutilation and suicidal gestures make safety the priority.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Borderline PD (PDF p. 264)

questions.stem: Intense fear of abandonment and unstable relationships suggest which disorder?
questions.rationale: Borderline PD features fear of abandonment, unstable intense relationships, and self-harm.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Borderline PD (PDF p. 264)

questions.stem: A client dresses provocatively at work and constantly seeks attention. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: For histrionic PD, give factual feedback, keep professional distance, and teach social skills.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Histrionic PD (PDF p. 264)

questions.stem: A client with narcissistic personality disorder insults the nurse's competence. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Use a matter-of-fact approach, do not internalize criticism, and set limits on rude behavior.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Narcissistic PD (PDF p. 264)

questions.stem: A client avoids social events for fear of criticism and feels inferior. Which disorder?
questions.rationale: Avoidant PD: social discomfort, low self-esteem, hypersensitivity, fear of rejection.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Avoidant PD (PDF p. 265)

questions.stem: What is the main goal for a client with dependent personality disorder?
questions.rationale: Foster self-reliance and teach problem-solving and decision-making skills.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dependent PD (PDF p. 265)

questions.stem: Repeated hand washing in OCD serves to:
questions.rationale: Compulsions are repetitive acts that attempt to neutralize the anxiety caused by obsessions.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Obsessive-Compulsive (PDF p. 265)

questions.stem: Which finding is expected in a client with anorexia nervosa?
questions.rationale: Anorexia causes amenorrhea, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, and cold intolerance.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anorexia Nervosa (PDF p. 265)

questions.stem: What is the initial treatment focus for a severely emaciated client with anorexia?
questions.rationale: Treatment first focuses on weight restoration, rehydration, and correcting electrolytes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Anorexia Treatment (PDF p. 266)

questions.stem: Which finding suggests self-induced vomiting in bulimia nervosa?
questions.rationale: Purging erodes dental enamel and causes caries, esophageal tears, and metabolic alkalosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bulimia Nervosa (PDF p. 266)

questions.stem: Frequent self-induced vomiting in bulimia leads to which acid-base imbalance?
questions.rationale: Vomiting loses gastric acid and causes metabolic alkalosis; laxative diarrhea causes acidosis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bulimia Nervosa (PDF p. 266)

questions.stem: Which nurse attitude is best during meals for a client with an eating disorder?
questions.rationale: Assume a calm, matter-of-fact attitude with positive expectations.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Eating Disorders (PDF p. 266)

questions.stem: Which is a negative (soft) symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.rationale: Negative symptoms include alogia, anhedonia, apathy, flat affect, and avolition.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Schizophrenia (PDF p. 267)

questions.stem: Schizophrenia requires disturbance in thought and perception for a minimum of:
questions.rationale: Schizophrenia: disturbance for at least 6 months, usually diagnosed in late adolescence or early adulthood.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Schizophrenia (PDF p. 267)

questions.stem: 'I'll take a pill on the hill if my name is Jill.' This speech pattern is:
questions.rationale: Clang associations link ideas by sound or rhyme rather than meaning.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Schizophrenia (PDF p. 268)

questions.stem: A client refuses food, saying the staff poisoned it. This is a:
questions.rationale: Persecutory delusions involve beliefs that others plan to harm, spy on, or poison the client.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Delusions (PDF p. 268)

questions.stem: A client says the news anchor is sending him private messages. This is:
questions.rationale: Ideas of reference: belief that broadcasts or articles have special meaning for the client.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Delusions (PDF p. 268)

questions.stem: A client stops abruptly mid-sentence and cannot continue the idea. This is:
questions.rationale: Thought blocking is abrupt stopping in the middle of a sentence or train of thought.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Changes in Communication (PDF p. 268)

questions.stem: A client believes others can hear what he is thinking. This is:
questions.rationale: Thought broadcasting: belief that others can hear or know the client's thoughts.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Changes in Communication (PDF p. 268)

questions.stem: A major depressive episode requires symptoms present nearly every day for:
questions.rationale: Major depression: depressed mood or loss of pleasure for at least 2 weeks.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mood Disorders (PDF p. 269)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: Which theory attributes depression to believing one has no control over the environment?
questions.rationale: Learned helplessness: mood disorder from the belief that one lacks control.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mood Disorder Theories (PDF p. 269)

questions.stem: How does hypomania differ from mania?
questions.rationale: Hypomania (about 4 days) is less severe; it does not impair functioning and has no psychotic features.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hypomania (PDF p. 270)

questions.stem: Major depressive episodes plus one or more hypomanic episodes, with no history of mania, indicate:
questions.rationale: Bipolar II: depression plus hypomania, never full mania; Bipolar I includes mania.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Bipolar Disorders (PDF p. 270)

questions.stem: Chronic, milder depressed mood lasting 2 years or more is:
questions.rationale: Dysthymia: at least 2 years of depressed mood less severe than major depression.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dysthymic Disorder (PDF p. 270)

questions.stem: Fall-onset seasonal affective disorder typically presents with:
questions.rationale: Winter SAD: hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving, weight gain; spring-onset has insomnia and weight loss.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Seasonal Affective Disorder (PDF p. 270)

questions.stem: A client starting lithium asks when it will work. The nurse says it usually takes about:
questions.rationale: Lithium's therapeutic effect becomes evident after about 10–14 days.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Lithium Therapy (PDF p. 271)

questions.stem: Which teaching helps prevent lithium toxicity?
questions.rationale: Adequate fluids and normal sodium intake; dehydration, sweating, or vomiting raise lithium levels.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Lithium Therapy (PDF p. 271)

questions.stem: A client on lithium has severe vomiting, diarrhea, and coarse tremors. The nurse should first:
questions.rationale: These are toxicity signs; hold lithium and report for serum level.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Lithium Therapy (PDF p. 271)

questions.stem: A manic client cannot sit long enough to eat. The nurse should provide:
questions.rationale: Provide frequent high-calorie, high-protein finger foods the client can eat while moving.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mania Interventions (PDF p. 271)

questions.stem: Which measure promotes sleep in a manic client?
questions.rationale: Reduce stimulation and establish a bedtime routine.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Mania Interventions (PDF p. 271)

questions.stem: Sudden blindness after a stressful event, with the client showing little concern, suggests:
questions.rationale: Conversion disorder shows sudden sensory or motor loss with 'la belle indifference.'
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Conversion Disorder (PDF p. 272)

questions.stem: Preoccupation with an imagined defect, such as crooked teeth, is:
questions.rationale: Body dysmorphic disorder: preoccupation with an imagined or exaggerated physical defect.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Body Dysmorphic Disorder (PDF p. 272)

questions.stem: A prisoner fakes back pain to avoid a court hearing. This is:
questions.rationale: Malingering is intentional symptom production for external incentives like avoiding prosecution.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Malingering (PDF p. 272)

questions.stem: A mother repeatedly makes her child ill to gain medical attention. This is:
questions.rationale: Munchausen by proxy: inflicting illness on another to gain attention; also child abuse.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Factitious Disorder (PDF p. 273)

questions.topicName: Concepts of Mental Health & Therapeutic Models
questions.stem: A client's family gives extra attention whenever he complains of pain. This illustrates:
questions.rationale: Secondary gain is an external benefit (attention); primary gain is relief of anxiety.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Psychosocial Theories (PDF p. 273)

questions.stem: Which approach is best for a client with somatization disorder?
questions.rationale: Show empathy, keep one provider to avoid doctor shopping, and avoid early confrontation and narcotics.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Somatoform Management (PDF p. 273)

questions.stem: Which is an emotion-focused coping strategy?
questions.rationale: Emotion-focused: relaxation, deep breathing, guided imagery, distraction; the rest are problem-focused.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Coping Strategies (PDF p. 274)

questions.stem: A client needs more alcohol to get the same effect. This is:
questions.rationale: Tolerance means needing more of a substance for the same effect.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Substance Abuse Terms (PDF p. 274)

questions.stem: A client functions while drinking but later has no memory of it. This is a:
questions.rationale: A blackout is functioning without conscious awareness or memory of behavior.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Substance Abuse Terms (PDF p. 274)

questions.stem: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms usually begin how long after the last drink?
questions.rationale: Withdrawal begins 4–12 hours after stopping and may last 1–2 weeks.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Alcohol Withdrawal (PDF p. 275)

questions.stem: Which drug class manages alcohol withdrawal?
questions.rationale: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) prevent seizures and DTs.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Alcohol Withdrawal (PDF p. 275)

questions.stem: A client on disulfiram drinks beer. Which reaction should the nurse expect?
questions.rationale: Alcohol with disulfiram causes flushing, throbbing headache, sweating, vomiting, and severe hypotension.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nursing Alert: Alcohol (PDF p. 280)

questions.stem: Chronic alcohol use with thiamine deficiency can cause:
questions.rationale: Long-term alcohol use causes Wernicke's encephalopathy, Korsakoff's psychosis, cirrhosis, and pancreatitis.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Long-Term Alcohol Effects (PDF p. 275)

questions.stem: Which sedative overdose is more likely to be fatal?
questions.rationale: Barbiturate overdose can cause coma, respiratory arrest, and death; benzodiazepine overdose alone is rarely fatal.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sedatives (PDF p. 276)

questions.stem: Why must barbiturate withdrawal be done by tapering?
questions.rationale: Abrupt barbiturate cessation can cause seizures and death; doses are tapered over days.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Sedative Detoxification (PDF p. 276)

questions.stem: A client with dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension, and hyperactivity most likely used:
questions.rationale: Stimulants cause euphoria, hypervigilance, dilated pupils, tachycardia, and hypertension.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stimulants (PDF p. 277)

questions.stem: During stimulant 'crash' withdrawal, the nurse should closely monitor for:
questions.rationale: Stimulant withdrawal causes marked dysphoria, fatigue, and depression with suicidal ideation.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Stimulant Withdrawal (PDF p. 277)

questions.stem: Bloodshot eyes, dry mouth, increased appetite, and inappropriate laughter suggest use of:
questions.rationale: Cannabis causes conjunctival injection, dry mouth, increased appetite, and time distortion.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Cannabis (PDF p. 277)

questions.stem: An unconscious client has pinpoint pupils and RR 6/min. Which drug should the nurse prepare?
questions.rationale: Naloxone, an opioid antagonist, reverses opioid intoxication; repeat doses may be needed.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Opioids (PDF p. 278)

questions.stem: Yawning, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and diarrhea indicate withdrawal from:
questions.rationale: Opioid withdrawal: lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, sweating, diarrhea, aches, and craving.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Opioid Withdrawal (PDF p. 278)

questions.stem: What is the role of methadone in heroin dependence?
questions.rationale: Methadone meets the physical need for opiates without producing craving for more.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Opiates Management (PDF p. 281)

questions.stem: Which drug blocks the effects of any opioid later taken?
questions.rationale: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that blocks the effects of ingested opioids.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Opiates Management (PDF p. 281)

questions.stem: Clonidine is given in opioid withdrawal mainly to relieve:
questions.rationale: Clonidine suppresses autonomic withdrawal effects, most effective against nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Opiates Management (PDF p. 281)

questions.stem: How is a psychotic reaction to a hallucinogen best managed?
questions.rationale: Treatment is supportive; psychotic reactions are managed best by isolation from stimuli.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hallucinogens (PDF p. 279)

questions.stem: Transient recurrence of perceptual disturbances weeks after LSD use is called:
questions.rationale: Hallucinogens can produce flashbacks, transient recurrences of perceptual disturbances.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Hallucinogens (PDF p. 279)

questions.stem: A teenager is found sniffing rugby glue and is drowsy. What is the treatment?
questions.rationale: No antidote exists for inhalants; support respiratory and cardiac function.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Inhalants (PDF p. 280)

questions.stem: The teenage child of an alcoholic father should be referred to:
questions.rationale: Alateen is for children of parents with substance problems; Al-Anon is for spouses and friends.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, AA Groups (PDF p. 280)

questions.stem: Alcoholics Anonymous is based on which philosophy?
questions.rationale: AA's 12-step program holds that total abstinence is essential, with peer support.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Alcoholics Anonymous (PDF p. 280)

questions.stem: Which vitamin is given to prevent Wernicke's syndrome in alcoholism?
questions.rationale: Thiamine prevents or treats Wernicke's and Korsakoff's syndromes.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Nursing Alert: Alcohol (PDF p. 280)

questions.stem: Which is a realistic goal for a client recovering from alcohol dependence?
questions.rationale: Set realistic, here-and-now goals such as staying sober today.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Substance Abuse Interventions (PDF p. 281)

questions.stem: A client is found in another city with a new name and no memory of her past. This is:
questions.rationale: Fugue: sudden travel away from home, inability to recall the past, possibly a new identity.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dissociative Disorders (PDF p. 281)

questions.stem: Dissociative identity disorder was formerly called:
questions.rationale: DID: two or more distinct identities that take control of behavior.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dissociative Disorders (PDF p. 281)

questions.stem: A client feels detached from her own body but knows it is not real. This is:
questions.rationale: Depersonalization: feeling detached from oneself with intact reality testing.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dissociative Disorders (PDF p. 282)

questions.stem: A client with a dissociative disorder begins a flashback. Which intervention helps?
questions.rationale: Grounding techniques remind the client she is in the present, an adult, and safe.
questions.sourceLabel: TRA Nursing Module, Dissociative Disorders Management (PDF p. 282)
